Earth is closed for materials but open to energy, fed by sunlight that arrives spread thin over the surface.

Inside those limits, a fossil-fuelled industrial system cannot last, and its replacements are hungry for land, materials, and power in their own right. Long-term survival would mean favouring carbon-based chemistry over purified metals, running at low power density, and keeping material throughput low. The authors call for life-compatible technology built on circular biogeochemical processes, and expect a shift toward a degrowth steady state to follow, the two changes reinforcing each other.
arxiv-2512-10980:
Akhmadillo Mamirov studies why large GPU clusters waste so much computing power while training and running AI systems. Real clusters often sit near half use because jobs fragment the available machines and static rules assign work poorly. He reviews these problems and proposes three dynamic schedulers that balance several goals at once.

The schedulers favour urgent work, fill gaps with jobs that fit, and group similar jobs together for better efficiency. In a controlled simulation with many mixed AI jobs, all three beat simple first-come and shortest-job rules on use, speed, fairness, and waiting. The best version sharply cut starvation, where jobs wait far too long. The results offer a practical base for production scheduling.
arxiv-2512-11480:
Weijian Ma, Shizhao Sun, Ruiyu Wang, and Jiang Bian present CADMorph, a system that edits a computer aided design by changing its shape while keeping its construction recipe valid. A CAD model is both a parametric sequence of steps and the geometry that sequence produces. Designers often want a new shape, which forces synchronised edits to the steps, with three demands: keep the structure, keep edits meaningful, and match the target shape.

CADMorph loops through planning, generation, and verification using two pretrained models. Attention maps from a shape predicting diffusion model pinpoint which segments must change. A masked prediction model fills those segments with valid edits. The shape model then embeds each candidate and picks the closest to the target. Both models train without edited example triplets, dodging a data bottleneck. The system beat a top commercial model and specialised baselines.
arxiv-2512-12080:
Ryan Po and co-authors present BAgger, a training scheme that stops video generators from drifting over time. Autoregressive video models predict frame by frame, training on clean context but running on their own output. Small errors compound, and quality rots as the clip lengthens, a flaw called exposure bias.

BAgger builds corrective training paths from the model own rollouts, teaching it to recover from its mistakes. Unlike distillation based fixes, it trains with standard score or flow matching losses, needs no giant teacher, and avoids backpropagating through long chains. On text to video, video extension, and multi prompt tasks, motion stayed steadier and scenes more consistent over long horizons.
arxiv-2512-12280:
Ivan Ruiz Manuel, Meijun Chen, Francesco Lombardi, and Stefan Pfenninger-Lee review long term energy system models in a 2025 paper. Such models map the best path for a nation's energy system over decades, often to reach net zero. Much work covers detail and openness, but little covers how the math setup itself can bias results.

The review looks at foresight choices, end effects that skew late years, detail trade-offs, and investment patterns. It surveys a large sample of studies at national scale or above, spanning many decades. The authors urge modelers to balance long term planning with fine detail. They also call for clearer reporting of design choices that can distort results.
arxiv-2512-12380:
Chiara Boiti and Renato Manfrin prove a new conservation law for a Kirchhoff type wave equation studied by Pokhozhaev. Conservation laws are quantities that stay fixed as a solution evolves, and they help control long term behavior. The law they find is of third order, involving higher derivatives of the solution.

They also show a stability result: if the solution's energy is small enough at the start, the L2 norms of its derivatives up to third order stay uniformly bounded for all time. That bound rules out wild growth in the solution's fine structure.
arxiv-2512-12880:
Mohammadmahdi Nouriborji, Morteza Rohanian, and Omid Rohanian work on recursive transformers, language models that reuse the same layers many times. Sharing layers shrinks the model, but it also makes each pass act too much alike. The model loses some of its range.

Their fix, Mixture of LoRAs, places small low-rank expert modules inside the shared feed-forward part. Each token can draw on a different mix of experts, without untying the main weights. Their modernized model, in sizes from 50 million to 120 million parameters, scored at the top among compact models on three test suites. An expert merging step also keeps use fast.
arxiv-2512-13180:
Emilie Charlier and Savinien Kreczman study positional numeration systems, ways of writing natural numbers with digits whose value depends on place. A core question is whether the set of all valid writings forms a regular language, one a simple finite machine can check.

A 1998 analysis tied this question to Renyi systems, which use a real base, but only when the original system had a dominant root. The authors prove a more general link to alternate base systems, which broaden the Renyi family. With that link they fully characterize which systems generate a regular language. They also reassess the older results and conjecture in light of the new picture.
arxiv-2512-13680:
Tianye Ding and co-authors present LASER, a training-free way to turn offline 3D reconstruction models into streaming systems. Strong feed-forward models like VGGT cannot process streaming video because memory grows quadratically. Past streaming fixes need heavy retraining and may waste those models' geometric strength.

LASER aligns predictions across consecutive time windows instead. Simple similarity alignment fails because monocular scale ambiguity shifts depth scales layer by layer between windows. Their layer-wise scale alignment splits depth into layers, computes a scale factor for each, and carries it across windows and times. Tests gave top results on camera pose and point maps, at 14 frames per second with 6 GB peak memory on an RTX A6000.
arxiv-2512-13880:
Geofrey Owino and Bernard Shibwabo Kasamani build a privacy-preserving system to classify infant cries. Cry classification can aid early assessment of a baby's needs, but audio data are private, recordings are noisy, and conditions shift across settings. Their pipeline is designed for real deployment under those limits.

It combines a denoising autoencoder, a convolutional tokenizer, and a Transformer encoder trained with federated learning across devices. On-device denoising, adaptive segmentation, calibration, and an out-of-distribution abstention step are built in. On Baby Chillanto and Donate-a-Cry data with ESC-50 noise added, the model reached a macro F1 of 0.938 and an AUC of 0.962. Per-round uploads fell from about 36 to 42 MB to 3.3 MB, and edge inference took 96 ms per frame.
arxiv-2512-14080:
Wentao Guo, Mayank Mishra, Xinle Cheng, Ion Stoica, and Tri Dao present SonicMoE in a 2025 paper on faster training for Mixture of Experts models. Such models split work among many small expert networks, which saves compute but can waste memory and chip time.

SonicMoE cuts the memory kept for the backward pass and designs graphics chip kernels that overlap data movement with math. A new token rounding method also cuts wasted padding in grouped matrix work. The team reports 45 percent less activation memory and 1.86 times the compute speed on Hopper chips for a fine grained 7 billion parameter model. All kernels are open source.
arxiv-2512-14180:
Francesco Di Sario and four coauthors propose Spherical Voronoi in a 2025 paper on appearance modeling for 3D Gaussian Splatting. That method renders new views of a scene from trained 3D data, but its usual spherical harmonics tool struggles with sharp signals and mirror like reflections.

Spherical Voronoi splits the sphere of directions into learnable regions with smooth borders, giving a stable way to store view dependent effects. For diffuse appearance it matches rival methods with simpler training. For reflections it acts as a set of learnable probes fed with reflected directions. Tests on synthetic and real data reach state of the art results, and the authors present it as a general fix for appearance in explicit 3D models.
arxiv-2512-14580:
Menno Demmenie, Stefan Kooij, and Daniel Bonn print objects out of ice using nothing but a fine jet of water and a vacuum chamber. Low pressure makes the jet evaporate fast, and evaporation steals heat, chilling the remaining water below freezing before it lands. Each new layer freezes almost on contact, so shapes build upward with no supports and no refrigeration equipment.

The team printed miniature Christmas trees, cones, upright pillars, and free-standing zigzags with fine detail. Beyond the charm, the trick is a clean demonstration of latent heat and pressure-driven freezing. Suggested uses range from ice templates for tiny fluid channels and tissue scaffolds to printing with local water on other worlds.
arxiv-2512-14880:
Darrin O'Brien, Dhikshith Gajulapalli, and Eric Xia show that the gap between a base AI model and its fine tuned version can be captured by simple linear math. Work on interpretability hints that models store such linear codes when nudged by prompts. Whether the same holds for full fine tuning was unknown.

The authors define a task matrix, a linear map that carries a base model's inner state to its fine tuned state. Across vision and text models and ten datasets, adding a task matrix beat simple probe methods and sometimes nearly matched full fine tuning. They also give a fast way to estimate the map from data, which transfers across domains. The result suggests fine tuning mostly rotates what a model already knows, rather than rewriting it.
arxiv-2512-14980:
Victor M. Yeom-Song and four coauthors improve diffusion models that generate solutions to partial differential equations. Such models learn from data what plausible solutions look like, then produce new ones. The physics can be enforced by adding penalty terms or by adjusting outputs during generation, but both tricks pull the model away from the true data pattern.

That pull is dangerous when the equation itself is slightly wrong, as often happens in practice. The authors instead bake soft guidance into the denoiser, the network at the heart of the model. The guidance comes from the structure of the equation, yet stays loose enough to bend when data disagrees. Tests show better compliance with the physics than standard denoisers, without losing that flexibility. The design suits tasks where the governing law is trusted but not perfect.
arxiv-2512-15280:
Misbah Shaheen and a coauthor test what happens when 3d transition metals are swapped into CsPbI3, a lead halide perovskite of interest for solar cells. Using spin polarized first principles calculations, they study each substituent's cost, its effect on the lattice, and its electronic footprint.

Most substitutions are energetically favorable and bend the lattice only near the defect, leaving the host intact. With the exception of scandium and titanium, the material resists forming deep traps, the mid gap states that ruin device performance. Instead, most dopants add resonant states that blend with the band edges, the mark of a defect tolerant material. The distortions follow Van Vleck modes driven by size mismatch and orbital overlap, and fade fast with distance. The study names which dopants are benign and which are harmful.
arxiv-2512-15380:
Isabela Santiago de Matos and five coauthors measure the expansion rate of the universe with a brand new cross check. Their method, Peak Sirens, cross correlates galaxy positions with gravitational wave distances. The peak of that cross spectrum, over redshift and luminosity distance, reveals the Hubble constant.

Using two gravitational wave events from the GWTC-3.0 catalog and the GLADE+ galaxy catalog, they detect the cross correlation peak for the first time, at 5.9 sigma confidence. Most of the signal comes from GW190814, the best localized event, at 3.4 sigma alone. Adding the famous GW170817 event, but deliberately ignoring its known redshift, gives a Hubble constant of 67. The errors run 18 up and 15 down, in kilometers per second per megaparsec. They also bound the gravitational wave bias below 4.3 at 95 percent confidence.
arxiv-2512-15580:
Romy Morin and co authors study bound states of quasiparticles trapped by a dip in the superconducting gap in a 2025 paper. Superconducting circuits hold far more quasiparticles than equilibrium theory predicts, and these excess particles drain energy from devices. Gap variations in disordered materials can trap them and reshape their energy spectrum.

The team models one shallow, disk shaped gap dip in a clean superconductor. A semiclassical treatment shows several bound states, with their number set by the size and depth of the dip. Beyond that regime, in more than one dimension, infinitely many bound states sit near the gap edge, even for a tiny trap. The results bear on how trapped quasiparticles recombine.
arxiv-2512-15880:
Beatrice Magni and co authors study anticoncentration and state design in doped real Clifford circuits in a 2025 paper. Clifford circuits are a basic, classically tractable family of quantum circuits. Adding small amounts of magic, the resource that makes quantum computation powerful, pushes them toward full quantum behavior, and the cost of that transition matters.

Using Weingarten calculus for the real Clifford group, the team derives the exact overlap distribution of real stabilizer states, a new universality class. Local real circuits recover that global statistic at logarithmic depth. A sharp hierarchy appears: recovering Haar statistics needs a polylogarithmic number of magic states, while full unitary Clifford statistics need only a single phase gate.
arxiv-2512-15980:
Yirui He and co authors present ClassLAR, a lightweight method for recovering Java modules from monolithic systems, in a 2025 paper. Large Java codebases are hard to reason about at class level alone, and the Java Platform Module System asks for explicit modules that most legacy projects lack. Existing architecture recovery tools recover those modules poorly.

ClassLAR uses language models to read semantic intent from fully qualified class and package names, capturing both structural and functional cues. Across 20 popular Java projects, it beats all state of the art techniques on architectural similarity measures. It also runs 3.99 to 10.50 times faster than those baselines, making module recovery practical at scale.
arxiv-2512-16080:
Tianyi Ma designs a new lending protocol in an arXiv paper on decentralized finance posted in 2025. Automated market makers let users lend and borrow through smart contracts without a bank in the middle. Fixed-income versions are hard to build because loans depend on time, and existing designs allow only one loan length.

Ma builds on a protocol called BondMM and argues its math can stretch to any maturity. The new design, BondMM-A, folds loans of many lengths into a single smart contract. That gives borrowers and liquidity providers more freedom and uses capital more efficiently. Experiments reported in the paper show stable interest rates and strong financial robustness. The work points toward richer bond-like markets on blockchains.
arxiv-2512-16180:
Sourabh Dube, Nilanjana Kumar, and Shriyansh Ranjan hunt for new particles on paper in a study that appeared on arXiv in 2025. They extend the standard model with a neutral fermion quintuplet and a scalar quadruplet, a package that can also generate neutrino masses. The heavy fermions would decay into standard model bosons through the new scalars.

The team focuses on pair production at the Large Hadron Collider for fermion masses from 700 to 1200 GeV. The decays yield highly boosted W and Z bosons that merge into single wide sprays called fatjets, plus multiple leptons. Doubly charged fermions get special attention for their larger production rate. Using jet substructure and tuned selection cuts, both search channels passed the 5-sigma discovery threshold under realistic conditions, even with a 50 percent background uncertainty at the full planned data volume.
arxiv-2512-16280:
Gilad Gressel and six co-authors investigate scam operations in an arXiv paper made public in 2025. Romance-baiting scams are run by organized syndicates that traffic people into forced labor. Victims are courted over weeks of texts, then pushed into fake cryptocurrency investments, causing heavy financial and emotional harm.

The team interviewed 145 insiders and 5 victims, ran a blinded week-long conversation study, and tested commercial safety filters. They found language models already widely used inside scam groups, with 87 percent of scam labor being systematized chat tasks open to automation. In the study, an AI agent won more trust and far higher compliance than human operators, 46 percent versus 18 percent. Popular safety filters detected 0.0 percent of the baiting dialogues. The authors warn these scams could be fully automated while defenses lag behind.
arxiv-2512-16680:
Gilles Felber proves a nontrivial bound for symplectic Kloosterman sums tied to the group Sp(2n). These sums, built from roots of unity, show up in the Petersson formula for Siegel modular forms, a higher-rank cousin of classic modular forms.

The bound covers moduli that are not a prime times the identity, a case past work left open. Such bounds matter because they control error terms when forms are averaged over families. As a use case, Felber applies the bound to how coprime symmetric pairs spread out, an equidistribution result. The work extends the analytic toolkit for automorphic forms on symplectic groups.
arxiv-2512-16880:
Valay Bundele, Mehran Hosseinzadeh, and Hendrik P. A. Lensch present ReMeDI-SAM3. It is a fix for surgical instrument tracking in endoscopy video. SAM3 is a strong video segmentation model. Surgery brings occlusions, fast motion, and tools that leave and return. Those traits break its memory.

ReMeDI adds three parts without retraining. The first is a relevance filter for memory, with a spare store for frames before occlusion. The second is an interpolation trick that stretches memory capacity. The third is a feature-based re-identification step with time voting. It restores tool identity after gaps. On EndoVis17, EndoVis18, and CholecSeg8k, in zero-shot use, scores rose by about 5.8, 8, and 2 percent over plain SAM3. That beat even trained rivals.
arxiv-2512-17180:
Maher Mesto and Francisco Cruz uncover a conservative bias in multi-teacher interactive reinforcement learning, where agents pick which expert to learn from. Given teachers with unlike reward structures, agents overwhelmingly chose the lowest-reward teacher, at a 93.16 percent selection rate, over one paying twenty times more.

Across 1,250 runs in navigation tasks, consistency beat optimality in teacher choice. The frame fails hard when teacher availability or accuracy drops below 0.6. Under concept drift it still beat baseline Q-learning by 159 percent. The authors see a mirror of human preference for safety and steadiness, with lessons for training robots in safety-critical work.
arxiv-2512-17880:
C. A. Breu, D. I. Pontin, E. Priest, and I. De Moortel ask why the Sun's outer air, the corona, is so much hotter than its surface. Bright loops of hot gas hang in magnetic fields there, and each loop is made of finer bright strands. Their work tests whether a loop is really one neat magnetic tube.

A detailed 3D simulation, rooted in a churning layer below the surface, says no. Bright strands form where heating, cooling, and gas flows happen to meet, not along one tidy tube. Thin sheets of strong current appear where fields from different sources touch. The picture blends two older ideas about how loops get their heat.
arxiv-2512-17980:
Akash Kumar Singh and five coauthors bring a classic math tool, the Laplace transform, to quantum computers. The transform is hard to run on quantum hardware because it shrinks signals rather than preserving them, unlike the quantum Fourier transform. Their method builds on eigenvalue reshaping tools and a recent scheme for fading dynamics.

For a grid of size N, their circuit uses a gate count that grows only like the cube of the log of N, a huge saving over the best classic method. The circuit stays narrow as well. A fast Laplace transform could open quantum methods for equations solved in that domain and for the ground states of odd matrices.
arxiv-2512-18080:
Marcos Ortiz leads a seven author team grading app building AI tools with human judges. Systems that turn a plain prompt into a working web app are spreading fast, but slick looks can hide weak function. The team gave 96 prompts to Replit, Bolt, and Firebase Studio, making 288 apps in all.

More than 200 raters then compared the apps in pairs, over a thousand checks in total, on ease of use, looks, completeness, and trust. Firebase Studio led on every count. Bolt looked strong but lagged on ease and trust, and Replit trailed both. The study warns that polish and reliability still part ways in this young field.
arxiv-2512-18180:
Rebecca Salganik, Guillaume Salha-Galvan, Yibin Wang, and Jian Kang address individual fairness in graph learning, the principle that similar people should be treated similarly by an algorithm. Existing methods assume similarity information is known for every pair of nodes, which rarely holds in practice. Their 2025 paper introduces FairExpand, a framework built for the realistic case where similarity is known only for a limited subset of pairs.

FairExpand alternates between two steps. One step refines node representations with a backbone model such as a graph neural network. The other gradually propagates the known similarity information outward, so fairness enforcement expands across the whole graph. Broad experiments show the method consistently improves individual fairness while preserving task performance. The authors present it as a practical route to fair graph models in high stakes settings such as user modeling, recommender systems, and search, where similarity data is always incomplete.
arxiv-2512-18580:
Yuan Zhou and four co-authors ask whether the gooey fluids microbes live in make their swimming more chaotic or more orderly. Microorganisms inhabit viscoelastic fluids full of polymers, nothing like plain water. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, runs lattice Boltzmann simulations of squirmer suspensions, model swimmers, swimming through polymer solutions.

At middle densities, the polymers strongly increase order. Polarization, the degree to which swimmers align, rises by up to a factor of 26 for neutral squirmers and 5 for pullers, compared with a plain Newtonian fluid. The mechanism is a feedback loop: squirmers stretch and align the polymers, and the aligned polymers push back through fluid and steric forces, reinforcing the swimmers' orientation. The team confirms the loop with an alignment measure that tracks polarization. The findings suggest ways to steer active matter by tuning the fluid.
arxiv-2512-18980:
Wei Peng, Jianchen Hu, Kang Liu, and Qiaozhu Zhai fix Bayesian optimization where it hurts most: high dimensions. Optimizing an expensive black box, like a simulation or a drug assay, usually relies on a Gaussian process surrogate, which collapses past a few hundred variables. Their method, OPBO, posted to arXiv in December 2025, keeps only what matters, the ranking of candidates, and learns it with a small neural network instead of fitting exact values.

Rather than hunting the single best point from an acquisition model, OPBO picks good-enough solutions from an ordinal set, cutting computation further. On problems past 500 dimensions it significantly beats both Gaussian-process and regression-network baselines, and the code is public. For engineers tuning vast design spaces, from chips to materials, an optimizer that survives high dimensions widens what is searchable at all.
arxiv-2512-19080:
Søren Eilers, Rune Johansen, Rasmus Veber Rasmussen, and Carsten Thomassen open a new coloring problem about touching boxes. Equal cuboids, integer-sized and placed in space, form a contact graph when two boxes touch. The chromatic number is the fewest colors that keep touching boxes different.

With rotations banned, they prove eight colors always suffice, and free rotation raises the safe bound to forty-eight. For cuboids with one side of length one, they get tighter bounds. Examples with high color needs narrow some cases to exact answers, though wide gaps remain. No known layout, of any size, forces more than six colors.
arxiv-2512-19380:
J. W. F. Venderbos revisits how insulators respond to outside prods, with Berry-phase polarization and orbital magnetization at center stage. Response coefficients tell how a solid's traits shift under a steady, uniform push. Clean formulas for them guide both theory and materials screening.

The author derives general formulas for the linear response of polarization and orbital magnetization to any static perturbation. Responses of any lattice-periodic trait, such as spin, get the same treatment, and Maxwell relations between paired coefficients follow. A new notion, Berry curvature response, links the pieces together. Shorter versions for two- and four-band models are given in band terms.
arxiv-2512-19480:
Eric Nilsson and Koenraad Schalm study how quantum critical matter conducts heat and charge when a lattice potential scrambles its momentum. Their two-dimensional theories break translation strongly, with a chemical potential that varies in space yet averages to zero. That missing average scale gives the systems odd, distinctive signatures.

Holographic models built on near-extremal black holes supply the answers. Currents sneak around obstacles, making the systems better conductors, not worse. Electrical transport looks like a bad metal while thermal transport mimics a Drude form it does not truly follow. At strong magnetic fields, resistance grows near-linearly, echoing effective medium theory.
arxiv-2512-19580:
Zhanybek Baitulenov, Maxim Olshanskii, Almas Temirbekov, and Nurlan Temirbekov modify a fictitious domain method for unsteady fluid flow around obstacles. The Brinkman penalization trick extends the flow equations over the whole box and punishes flow inside solid regions. That avoids body-fitted meshes, which are slow and hard to build. A continuation in the lower-order terms steers the hard nonlinear problem, step by step, toward the true one.

The new twist lets the key parameter depend on the solution itself, not on a fixed guess made at the start. Global existence and convergence of weak solutions are proved. Local strong solutions come with a fresh, higher-order rate in the penalization parameter. A divergence-free finite element pairing keeps mass exactly conserved at each step. One test case shows the method at work on a real flow.
arxiv-2512-20180:
Zeev Nutov and Anael Vaknin study covering problems in graph methods through the lens of set families. A family is called disjointness-compliable when, for any set in it, removing part of that set leaves a piece that is still in the family. Famous problems such as k-minimum spanning tree and group Steiner fit this pattern without being symmetric.

The authors prove that every such covering problem admits an approximation guarantee tied to the number of minimal sets in the family. Consequences include the first deterministic polynomial-time logarithmic approximation for generalized point-to-point connection, plus a bound for multiroot covering Steiner. They also analyze parameterized complexity, showing fixed-parameter tractable methods for the symmetric case. The approach unifies results that were previously proved problem by problem.
arxiv-2512-20680: Johannes Hofscheier and Alexander Kasprzyk present a famous open question about lattice polytopes, posed by Tadao Oda at Oberwolfach in 1997. The integer decomposition property asks whether points in multiples of a lattice polytope always split into sums of points in the shape itself. Oda asked whether smoothness of the shape alone ensures it. The 2D case motivates the question, including an elegant proof of Pick's theorem relating a lattice polygon's area to its interior and boundary points.
arxiv-2512-20780:
Ramatu Oiza Abdulsalam and Segun Aroyehun compare how humans and chatbots tutor mathematics. Expert tutors, novice tutors, and seven large language models all answered the same student mistakes in remedial math dialogues. The team scored teaching moves such as pressing for reasoning and restating student ideas, plus features of word choice and tone.

Experts beat novices, and larger models scored near the experts on average quality. Still, the models leaned less on the discussion moves experts favor, while writing longer and more polite replies. Extra politeness and strong self-directed language actually tracked with lower ratings. The study argues that judging tutoring takes more than checking final answers.
arxiv-2512-21080:
Enoch Hyunwook Kang settles when a panel of language-model personas may stand in for human subjects. Field experiments are the gold standard for benchmarking algorithms that act on society, but they are slow and expensive, and persona simulation is a tempting shortcut. Kang proves an exact characterization. If methods see only aggregate outcomes, and the evaluation is blind to which method produced an artifact, then swapping humans for personas is a change of panel. It is no different from moving the study from New York to Jakarta.

Validity is only half the question, so the analysis continues to usefulness. Defining the discriminability of the aggregate channel information-theoretically, Kang shows that matching a field experiment's decision quality is fundamentally a sample-size problem. He derives explicit bounds on how many independent persona evaluations a benchmark needs. That count is what lets a benchmark tell meaningfully different methods apart.
arxiv-2512-21380:
By the time most defenses react, the attack has already happened. Mohammad Hammas Saeed and Howie Huang's SENTINEL listens earlier, in the public Telegram channels where attack tools circulate and experts trade warnings. Sixteen security and open-source-intelligence channels supplied some 365,000 messages for the study.

SENTINEL fuses two signal kinds: what people say, modeled with large language models, and how they coordinate, captured by graph neural networks. Matching those signals against real-world attacks reached an F1 score of 0.89, strong evidence that chatter precedes incidents in usable ways. For threat-intelligence teams, the framework offers a template for turning social noise into lead time.
arxiv-2512-21780:
Qikang Feng, Yang Huang, Huawei Zhang, and Jifeng Liu measure the Milky Way's rotation curve using classical Cepheid stars observed by the Gaia satellite. The rotation curve, orbital speed against distance from the Galactic center, weighs the Galaxy and probes its dark matter. Cepheids are ideal tracers because their pulsation period reveals their true brightness, hence their distance.

From nine hundred three carefully selected Cepheids with precise motions from Gaia's third data release, the authors compute the curve between six and eighteen kiloparsecs. It declines slightly overall, with a dip near ten to eleven kiloparsecs and a bump near thirteen to fourteen. Averaging with earlier measurements, they find a circular speed at the Sun's position of about two hundred thirty-seven kilometers per second. Their mass model also estimates the local dark matter density and enclosed halo mass.
arxiv-2512-21980:
Multiplying three-by-three matrices over a general non-commutative ring can be done with twenty-three multiplications, and the remaining cost is additions. A. I. Perminov presents a rank-23 scheme using only fifty-eight scalar additions, improving the previous best of sixty additions achieved without a change of basis.

The scheme came from an automated search combining ternary-restricted flip-graph exploration with greedy intersection reduction for common subexpression elimination. All its coefficients are minus one, zero, or one, which keeps it efficient and portable across arbitrary fields. The total scalar operation count drops from eighty-three to eighty-one. For a problem where progress is measured one addition at a time, the result sets a new state of the art for exact three-by-three multiplication.
arxiv-2512-22080:
Koyena Ghosh, Suchismita Banerjee, Urna Basu, and Banasri Basu ask how tightly air pollution and weather move together in Indian cities. They build a statistical system that measures dependence between pollutants and weather variables in both snapshot and time-based ways. Cities can then be grouped by the overall strength of that coupling, giving a map of distinct interaction regimes.

The method blends linear and nonlinear measures, including Pearson correlation, mutual information, and relative conditional entropy. Principal component analysis folds these into one interpretable score per pollutant and weather pair, then per city. Robustness checks that drop one variable pair at a time change little. Over time, humidity tends to lead pollutant changes, temperature tends to lag, and links fade quickly.
arxiv-2512-22180:
Alexander K. Chen asks whether the powerful phones in everyone's pockets could help train machine learning models at no extra cost. Training large models normally demands a serious compute setup, which shuts out people in restricted environments. Cloud rental is not always an option either, because data may be private or expected usage costly. Recent iPhones carry surprisingly strong processors that mostly sit idle.

Chen presents a proof-of-concept system that harnesses an iOS phone through distributed pipeline parallelism, splitting a model across devices. It speeds up modest model training, batch inference, and agentic tool use in a weaker local setup. The paper also faces the obstacles honestly: tight memory, thermal throttling, and the phone operating system's sandbox all limit what is possible.
arxiv-2512-23080:
Tim Pearce and Ahmed Ibrahim built a generative system for inventing new odorant molecules, the scent ingredients behind fragrances. Searching chemical space for structures that smell right is slow, and generative models usually need large training sets that perfumery cannot supply. Their framework couples a variational autoencoder with a QSAR model, a quantitative predictor linking molecular structure to odor likelihood.

The autoencoder first learns the grammar of molecular strings from the broad ChEMBL database. Its training objective then adds a term from the QSAR model, so its internal map organizes molecules by odor probability. Generated structures were uniformly valid after rejection sampling, and mostly unique. Scaffold analysis found thousands of ring candidates built on over a thousand core frameworks never seen in training. An ablation study showed the QSAR guidance mainly multiplies how many new compounds appear near a known odorant seed, rather than making each compound more odor-like.
arxiv-2512-23280:
Jiahao Zhu and co-authors target a sneaky form of false advertising in Chinese e-commerce livestreams. Hosts on platforms like Douyin pronounce words in altered forms, called morphs, so automated monitors miss banned or exaggerated claims, a problem concentrated in health and medical streams. Earlier morph research chased text-based tricks; this study defines a new task, Live Auditory Morph Resolution, for the spoken version.

The team built a dataset for the task, with more than eighty-six thousand samples, and reframed morph resolution as a text-to-text generation problem that language models can learn. Using large language models to generate training data improved performance. The results show that resolving morphs strengthens livestream regulation. A monitor that understands what a host said, beneath the disguise, can flag the false advertising that pronunciation games were designed to hide. The work gives platforms and regulators a detection target.
arxiv-2512-23480:
Toqeer Ali Syed and four co-authors argue that software supply chains need active defense, not just record keeping. Tools such as SLSA and software bills of materials prove where code came from, but they cannot find or remove vulnerabilities during production. Attacks increasingly target the trusted build and delivery steps themselves.

Their framework combines language-model agents that reason about code, reinforcement learning that balances security against build delays, and a blockchain ledger that records every action for auditing. The agents plug into real pipelines on GitHub Actions and Jenkins through a standard protocol. In tests covering injection attacks, unsafe deserialization, and access-control faults, the system detected more problems and mitigated them faster than rule-based or provenance-only baselines.
arxiv-2512-23880:
Xu Huang and five co-authors build a scientific agent that teaches itself new tools. Language model agents usually arrive with a fixed toolbox, which caps what they can do on complex research tasks. CASCADE instead acquires skills: through two meta-skills, continuous learning from web search, code extraction, and memory. Self-reflection through introspection and knowledge graph exploration, it masters external tools and codifies what it learns as reusable skills.

The test bed, SciSkillBench, holds over a hundred materials science and chemistry research tasks. With evolution mechanisms switched on, CASCADE succeeded on over ninety percent of them, against roughly a third without. The authors further show computational analyses, autonomous laboratory experiments, and selective reproductions of published papers. Because accumulated skills are executable artifacts, they can be shared between agents and human scientists alike.
arxiv-2512-24280:
S Shukla and P C Srivastava compute the structure of heavy lead nuclei. The isotopes run from lead-184 to lead-194. The tool is the nuclear shell model. Two effective interactions drive the calculations. Their names are KHH7B and KHHE. Both are standard choices for this region of the nuclear chart.

Energy spectra come first among the results. Electromagnetic properties follow in detail. Quadrupole and magnetic moments are reported. So are E2 and M1 transition strengths. Each prediction is compared with available experimental data. Isomeric states receive special attention. Their half-lives are computed within the same framework. Seniority quantum numbers are reported for those isomers as well. The study tests how far the shell model reaches in neutron-deficient lead. Agreement and disagreement with data both instruct nuclear theorists.
arxiv-2512-24780:
Alan Oursland gives a direct explanation for why distance-based neural models act like chance-based inference systems, showing soft clustering, model focus, and uncertainty tracking. Loose analogies to mixture models were the usual account. For any objective with a log-sum-exp form over spans or energies, he derives an exact identity.

The gradient for each distance equals the negative posterior responsibility of its part, the same quantity an expectation-maximization step would use. Gradient descent therefore acts as implicit expectation-maximization. Readers get a firm math bridge between neural training and classic data-based inference, rather than a suggestive resemblance between the two.
arxiv-2601-00080:
Yazeed Tawalbeh and co-author Mauro F Pereira model how a magnetic field can steer the size of silver nanoparticles as they form. Their 2026 study works inside classical nucleation theory, joined with a sphere-packing picture of how atoms assemble. The field adds a magnetic term to the free energy through the material's magnetic susceptibility, giving a closed-form link between particle radius and field strength.

The model reproduces the observed shrink in the most likely particle size as field strength grows, under both field orientations relative to the stirring plane. Across the full range tested, predictions stay consistent with measurements taken during continuous stirring. The authors read this as support for the idea that the field reshapes the nucleation energy landscape itself. Within the limits of the classical picture, they offer a transparent and cheap framework for choosing field conditions to select nanoparticle size.
arxiv-2601-00680:
Tu Anh Dinh and Jan Niehues explain why a language model's own probabilities are a poor judge of translation quality. Natural language is ambiguous, so several different outputs can all be correct, yet the model's softmax output forces probability to be split among them, making good answers look unlikely. Training data with a single reference answer reinforces the same bias.

Their fix is a small extra module, the Sigmoid Head, trained for quality estimation on top of a pre-trained model. Its sigmoid activation lets several options score highly at once, unlike softmax. A heuristic negative sampling scheme supplies the training signal for the second problem. The goal is a quality estimate that respects legitimate ambiguity instead of punishing it.
arxiv-2601-00880:
Anthony Mikinka is the sole author of a 2026 paper that turns prompt crafting for AI models into a formal system. Prompts are the written instructions users give a model. Mikinka's system, named Universal Conditional Logic, gives prompts a maths of their own. It scores how much structure a prompt carries. Past a set point, he finds, more structure starts to hurt.

He calls that twist the Over-Specification Paradox. In tests with three hundred five cases, eleven models, and four rounds. His system cut token use by near thirty in each hundred. The cut was steady and large by standard stats tests. But the best setup changed from model family to model family. One model needed its own tuned version to do well. The paper frames prompt work as a field that can be measured, not just felt. It also warns that one size will not fit all models.
arxiv-2601-01180:
Rabinovich, Biham, and Katzav study how traffic sorts itself out in a simple grid model with few cars. Their paper revisits a two-way model where some cars move right and others move down on a square board. Below a key density, traffic ends in a free, repeating flow.

In that calm state, the two kinds of cars split into neat diagonal bands and move without blocking each other. The authors create a distance measure to track how fast a random start reaches that state. Motion within bands settles fast, while mixing between bands fades far more slowly, in a pattern shaped by the board size.
arxiv-2601-01580:
Zhao and 3 co-authors ask why training by reward makes large language models start checking their own work. After such training, models often pause, spot a flaw, and revise, while models trained only to copy answers do so far less. The team splits the model's policy into two roles: one samples answers, and one decides whether to revise.

They prove reward training spreads its push evenly across both roles, while copying-based training and common penalty terms do not. Length weighting can hold back the sampling role and leave the deciding role undertrained. Tests on arithmetic reasoning support the theory, pointing to better decisions, not better sampling, as the main gain.
arxiv-2601-01680:
Recognizing the faces of babies and toddlers is unusually hard for software, because young faces change fast and look much alike. Afzal Hossain, Mst Rumana Sumi, and Stephanie Schuckers test four well-known deep learning face models. Their new dataset was gathered over twenty-four months, in seven sessions. It covers children aged zero to three years.

Accuracy was poor for infants under six months. Only about thirty-one percent of true matches passed at a strict false-accept setting. By age three, the rate had climbed to about sixty-five percent. Longer gaps between photos hurt performance as features drifted. A domain-adversarial training method recovered more than twelve percent, pointing toward more reliable child identification for health and safety uses.
arxiv-2601-01980:
The Square Kilometre Array telescope will produce data volumes too large to haul to central computers. Manuel Parra-Royón and ten co-authors propose the reverse for the SKA Regional Centres Network: send lightweight functions to wherever the data already lives, and let an intelligent planner decide the execution.

The planner uses multi-objective evolutionary algorithms to search for execution plans balancing runtime and energy use against data location and transfer costs, within a function-as-a-service architecture that hides infrastructure management. The paper establishes a baseline framework for computation-to-data strategies in a near-exascale setting. As data gravity grows across science, knowing when to move code instead of data becomes a central operational skill.
arxiv-2601-02280:
Under pressure, the material UTe2 becomes a superconductor in two different phases, and Devi Vijayan Ambika and co authors probe the magnetism behind that split. In one phase the transition temperature falls as pressure rises, while in the other it climbs. Earlier nuclear magnetic resonance work hinted that two kinds of spin fluctuations, ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic, might both be present.

The team measured a single crystal with tellurium NMR at pressures up to about two gigapascals, watching how spin relaxation and the Knight shift change with temperature and field direction. Relaxation grows in the pattern expected when antiferromagnetic fluctuations get stronger under pressure. They suggest ferromagnetic fluctuations favor the first phase, while the strengthened antiferromagnetic kind is key to the second.
arxiv-2601-02580:
Christopher Ormerod finds a cheaper way to calibrate test questions, estimating how hard an item is and how well it separates strong from weak students. Standard item response theory needs expensive field testing with real students before those numbers exist. His approach fine tunes large language models to imitate student responses at many stated ability levels, then reads the calibration off the simulated answers.

Using the Qwen-3 model series with low rank adaptation, the models answer multiple choice questions conditioned on a discrete ability description. Plotting the chance of a correct answer against ability reconstructs the item characteristic curve, from which the theory's parameters follow. On grade six English items and a shared task data set, the synthetic calibration competes with or beats baseline methods. The work suggests test developers could pre calibrate items before any student sees them.
arxiv-2601-02880:
Abhishek HS and three co-authors present ReTreVal, a framework that helps large language models learn from their own reasoning mistakes without any retraining. Existing methods throw away everything learned from failed attempts when a new problem starts. ReTreVal instead explores a tree of reasoning paths, checks nodes with tools, and carries categorized error notes into the branch it retries.

A self-rewriting memory stores strategies across problems and updates them as new problems arrive, so later questions benefit from earlier ones. On a five hundred problem math benchmark the framework reached about eighty-six percent accuracy, well above plain chain-of-thought prompting and a strong self-refine baseline. It also gained on a broad knowledge test, with wins far outnumbering regressions.
arxiv-2601-02980:
Bao-Jun Cai, Bao-An Li, and Yu-Gang Ma sharpen a theoretical limit on how stiff matter inside a neutron star can be. The key quantity is the ratio of pressure to energy density at the center of the most massive possible neutron star, which caps that ratio for all cold visible matter. Because general relativity makes the underlying equations nonlinear, the true cap sits far below the naive special-relativity limit of one.

Building on a causality-only bound, the authors add a mass-sphere stability condition drawn from their perturbative analysis of the stellar structure equations. The combined constraints give an improved upper bound of about 0.385 for the central ratio, slightly above the earlier value and fully consistent with it. They also derive a better scaling relation for neutron star compactness.
arxiv-2601-03180:
Jiri Adamek answers an open problem in category theory about the algebraic structures that live on metric spaces. Varieties of quantitative algebras are fully described by their free-algebra monads on the category of metric spaces. The question was whether those monads are exactly the strongly finitary ones, the ones determined by their values on finite discrete spaces.

Adamek presents a counterexample: the variety of algebras with two close binary operations yields a monad that is not strongly finitary. He then gives the correct characterization: the free-algebra monads of varieties are the 1-basic monads, weighted colimits of strongly finitary ones. A striking consequence follows: strongly finitary endofunctors on metric spaces are not closed under composition.
arxiv-2601-03380:
Xiongping Dai and three co-authors study when maps between dynamical systems are semi-open, a weakening of openness that still guarantees images of open sets have interior. The maps in question are extensions between minimal semiflows on compact spaces, together with the induced maps between their spaces of Borel probability measures. The tools are the structure theory of semiflow extensions and inverse limit techniques.

Three main results emerge. For extensions of minimal flows, the induced measure map is always semi-open. For quasi-separable fiber-onto extensions of minimal semiflows, both the map and its induced map are semi-open. And when the target space is metrizable, the map is semi-open exactly when its induced map is. A further result for topological groups generalizes Pontryagin's classical open mapping theorem.
arxiv-2601-03480:
Apu Chandra Das and five co-authors work on a common clinical trial problem: how to borrow data from outside a trial without biasing its results. External control patients can sharpen estimates, but their traits and outcome spread may differ from the trial's own patients. The proposed method, shortened to PSW-BPP, joins two tools to manage that balance carefully.

First, propensity score weighting aligns the outside group's traits with the trial group's. Then a Bayesian power prior borrows information in parts, letting the mean and the variance borrow at different rates. A plausibility index helps calibrate how much borrowing is safe. Done well, borrowing can make trials more efficient without pretending unlike populations are the same, a real concern for patients and regulators alike.
arxiv-2601-03680:
Tenta Dougome and six co-authors train machine learning models to map dust temperature in the Orion A molecular cloud from molecular line data alone. Traditionally, astronomers need observations in several continuum bands to derive dust temperature, and such data are not always available. The team instead used emission lines from carbon monoxide variants to teach models the temperature pattern.

They found that training on only about five percent of the region's pixels already gave accurate predictions. The training sample also had to span the full temperature range and mirror the region's overall distribution. The ratio between two carbon monoxide forms often carried strong predictive weight. Reliable temperature maps from line data alone could extend thermal studies to clouds lacking full continuum coverage.
arxiv-2601-03780:
Md Ahasanuzzaman and four co-authors check whether popular code generation benchmarks actually represent the programming concepts used in real projects. Benchmarks like HumanEval drive model rankings, but a benchmark exercising only a narrow slice of a language can mislead. The team uses Knowledge Units, cohesive bundles of language capability tied to specific constructs and libraries, as their measuring lens.

They mapped Knowledge Unit coverage in two Python benchmarks, HumanEval and MBPP, and compared it with thirty real-world Python projects. Each benchmark covered only about half of the twenty units identified. That gap means high scores can coexist with untested weaknesses in everyday programming skills. The study gives benchmark designers a concrete audit method and a warning label for anyone reading leaderboard numbers as general coding competence.
arxiv-2601-06680:
Tomasz Kania and Jerzy Kakol study amenability constants for Banach algebra sums in 2026. Their subject is Johnson amenability for unconditional direct sums. A family of Banach algebras is summed over an index set.

A Banach sequence lattice on that index set defines the sum's norm. The E-sum collects the algebras with sizes controlled by that lattice. Amenability measures how well an algebra supports averaging and derivations. Constants quantify that amenability rather than merely asserting it exists. For infinite sums, the constants can blow up or stay tame. Their analysis tracks that behavior across unconditional sums of algebras. Functional analysts get precise control over a basic construction. Such sums appear wherever systems combine many independent algebraic parts.
arxiv-2601-07080:
Research by Mohammad Farhat and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with magma ocean waves and thermal variability on lava worlds. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Lava worlds are rocky planets with dayside skins made molten by stellar irradiation. Tidal heating on these shortest-period planets is more than skin deep.

The authors show how orbital eccentricities of just. A few percent (within current observed bounds and maintained secularly by exterior companions) can create deep magma oceans. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07480:
Yi-Long Luo and Jing-Xin Nie prove that mixture gas equations keep a well-defined notion of solution for large data. Their 2026 preprint studies renormalized solutions to Boltzmann systems for mixtures of monatomic and polyatomic gases. The work follows the DiPerna-Lions approach to these kinetic equations. Distribution functions describe each species. For polyatomic species, the function also carries a continuous internal energy variable.

Renormalized solutions made the Boltzmann equation tractable when classical solutions may not exist. Extending that theory to mixtures with internal energy widens its reach. Real gases in engineering and atmospheric science are mixtures, not single species. The Cauchy problem studied here starts from initial data and asks for solutions for all later times. The paper serves analysts working on kinetic theory. It strengthens the foundation under gas mixture simulations.
arxiv-2601-07880:
Gal Engelberg and colleagues benchmark AI agents on basic questions about identity security. Identity Security Posture Management is a core challenge for firms running cloud and software services. Simple visibility questions ask what identities exist and whether their configuration is hygienic. Answering them requires interpreting complex identity data. Agentic AI systems are a growing candidate for that work. Their 2026 preprint introduces a benchmark for this visibility task.

A benchmark gives vendors and buyers a shared yardstick. Without one, claims about agent competence in security operations stay untested. Identity data is messy, spread across many systems with overlapping accounts. The benchmark focuses on visibility, the foundation for any later remediation. Security teams evaluating AI agents are the readers. The paper helps them ask whether an agent truly sees their identity landscape.
arxiv-2601-08080: Ariel Chitan, Sarah Gallagher, and Shahram Abbassi simulate a pair of supermassive black holes over 250 years. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies OJ287, a bright and nearby candidate binary at redshift 0.3. New facilities may soon catch light and gravitational wave signals from such pairs. Long runs are needed to track how accretion drives changes in brightness over time. The simulation follows that slow, accretion-driven variability across two and a half centuries. It gives observers a long baseline for a system often watched for outbursts.
arxiv-2601-08280: Angshul Majumdar argues that greedy selection suffices for finding useful actions in agentic language models. The 2026 arXiv paper notes that modern agent systems face extremely large action spaces. Tool-augmented models may hold thousands of available APIs or retrieval operations. Empirical evidence suggests only a small subset of actions truly moves performance in a given deployment. Sparse action discovery aims to find that subset cheaply. If greedy search finds it, agents could skip costly exploration and run leaner in production settings.
arxiv-2601-08980:
M. Sanchez-Garcia and a large team map star birth in near bright galaxies that shine strong in heat rays. Such galaxies are oft two galaxies in a crash. The team looks at gas cloud scale, near a span of a few score parsecs. They use a set of near bright cases at all crash stages, from lone to late merge.

They track how gas traits link to star birth rate in each cloud zone. Crash stage may bend those links as gas is squeezed and torn. A reader in galaxy work gets a cloud scale view across a full crash path. It can show when a crash helps stars form, and when it starts to tear clouds apart.
arxiv-2601-09080:
Yufei Li, Zeguang Liu, and Kehe Zhu link a deep zero ask in function work to a famed guess in time and rate work. The zero ask is by Hedenmalm. It asks where a class of smooth functions can be forced to be zero, and what that says of the whole class. The guess is the HRT conjecture, a long open claim on shifts of a function in time and rate.

The team shows the two are kin in a direct way. That kin lets them prove yes for the zero ask and for like asks near it. A reader in pure math gets a bridge that pays at once. A hard guess in one field can lend its strength to a deep ask in a next.
arxiv-2601-09380:
Haohao Shi and five co-authors ask how large LED lighting systems should be serviced. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a semi-physical model of how LED installations wear out over time. Two failure modes drive the decay: slow package degradation and sudden driver outages.

What counts as failure here is not a dead lamp but light levels that break set rules across space and time. The authors use a gamma-process model for the gradual decay. Around it they build a simulation-based plan for opportunistic maintenance, fixing parts when crews are already on site. The goal is compliant light at lower service cost.
arxiv-2601-09580:
A. Ballester-Bolinches, R. Esteban-Romero, L. A. Kurdachenko, and V. Pérez-Calabuig continue a study of highly symmetric algebraic structures called braces. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at Dedekind left braces, where every subbrace is an ideal. Braces blend two group operations and link to solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation.

The authors focus on Dedekind braces whose additive group is non-periodic. A prior paper began the classification; this one pushes it further. Knowing when all substructures are ideals reveals how rigid the brace must be. Such rigidity results help organize the growing zoo of brace examples.
arxiv-2601-09780:
T. J. L. C. Bakx and a large team listen for oxygen light from dusty galaxies in the early universe. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports [O III] 88-micron observations of four Herschel-selected dusty star-forming galaxies. The galaxies sit at redshifts 2.9 to 4 and shine with extreme infrared luminosity.

The Atacama Compact Array took the spectra in its Bands 9 and 10. The oxygen line traces hot, ionized gas inside these hidden star factories. Dust blocks their visible light, so far-infrared lines are a prime window. The measurements test how fast such galaxies formed stars when the universe was young.
arxiv-2601-10280:
Antonio Celentano, David Krejčiřík, and Vladimir Lotoreichik tune a bound state in a curved plane. The plane is hyperbolic, where lines bend out. They cut a bounded shape out of it. On the cut edge, a Robin rule ties the value to its slope.

They ask when a bound state sits below the main band. The main band starts at one fourth. With a convex cut shape, such states exist just when the Robin term sits below a set point. That point is at or below zero and rests on the shape. The work sorts when the edge can trap a wave.
arxiv-2601-10380:
Shrigyan Brahmachari, Shuchen Zhu, Iman Marvian, and Yu Tong learn the rule of a quantum rig at the best rate. Each rig is ruled by its Hamiltonian. To know it is key for sensors and chip checks. The best learn rate is named the Heisenberg limit. Past plans hit it with a cost.

Some plans need joint moves on many qubits, which are noise prone. Some need fields that grow as the goal gets fine. The team give a plan with fixed single qubit fields. It hits the top rate with no such growth. That makes it fit for the chips of today.
arxiv-2601-10580:
Wessel Poelman and Miryam de Lhoneux study how we judge language models that work in more than one language. Scores such as perplexity and bits-per-character are easy to use for one language. The authors argue that these scores rest on hidden assumptions once many languages are involved. Their 2026 arXiv preprint looks at what these measures really capture.

The paper asks what form and meaning each score reflects when text is compared across languages. A score that looks fair in one language may treat another language in a skewed way. The authors work through those assumptions one by one. Readers who build or test multilingual models get a clear warning about what the common scores can and cannot show.
arxiv-2601-10780:
Nursultan Daupayev, Christian Engel, Ricky Bendyk, and Sören Hirsch design an adaptive algorithm for environmental microsensors. Steady sensing matters for jobs like anomaly detection in building structures. But collecting data at a fixed rate wastes energy and piles up redundant readings. Deleting data to save space costs quality instead.

Their algorithm adapts how the sensor samples, so it gathers more when conditions change and less when they are flat. Smarter timing cuts energy use and storage load at the source. The work targets long-lived sensor networks that must run for years on small batteries. It shows how a little on-device judgment can stretch both power and data value.
arxiv-2601-11080:
Stephan G. Heinemann, Jens Pomoell, and Manuela Temmer analyze the magnetic shape of observed coronal holes. Coronal holes are dark patches where the Sun's field opens into space and the solar wind escapes. Potential Field Source Surface models map that field and feed solar wind forecasts. Yet the models often fail to match the holes actually observed.

The team studies 702 coronal holes seen between 2010 and 2019. They compute matching field extrapolations and compare topology and loop statistics with quiet Sun regions. Where model and data part ways, forecasters learn their error bars. Better coronal maps mean better warnings for the space weather that can disturb satellites and power grids.
arxiv-2601-11380:
B. Sicardy and L. Dettwiller study central flashes in stellar occultations. Their 2026 preprint works out what shapes those flashes. An occultation is when a solar system body blocks a star. At the center of the shadow, light can flash bright.

The flash comes from air around the body bending starlight. The team catalogs diffraction effects on that flash. They treat stars as points and light as monochromatic waves. Cases cover clear spherical air shells of unlike forms. They also add corrections for stars with real size. A star's disk blurs the flash in set ways. The catalog helps read real flashes from moons and planets.
arxiv-2601-11480:
Riya Baruah and four coauthors probe heat and work in a quantum resonator. Their 2026 preprint deals with a driven resonator system. A heat engine needs a working fluid to turn heat into work. At the nanoscale, that fluid can be a quantum system.

Quantum behavior there is non-classical in key ways. A quantum resonator is a flexible such working fluid. It allows precise control of the system's state. It also couples cleanly to thermal reservoirs on both sides. Fluctuations of heat and work are the focus here. At small scales, those fluctuations can rival the means. The study maps them for driven resonator engines.
arxiv-2601-11780: Members of the ATLAS team report a test of top quark pair output near its birth threshold. They use proton-proton crashes at 13 TeV at the Large Hadron Collider. They look at end states with two charged leptons and many jets, near a pair mass of about 345 GeV. Near the threshold, the pair can act in ways that boost the count. The title reports a rise in the rate near that point. Such a rise tests how quarks bind for a brief time.
arxiv-2601-11880:
Yingxiao Zhang, Jiaxin Duan, Junfu Zhang, and Ke Feng make fake treasury futures data with a diffusion transformer. Such models have done well at fake stock and order flow data. Their skill on treasury futures was less clear.

Treasury futures data have low volume, links to the wider market, and grouped links among their fields. The team's model, named TF-CoDiT in the work, is built for a set state or class. Good fake data can aid tests of trade and risk tools. It can stand in where real data are scarce or private.
arxiv-2601-11980:
A team of physicists gauge neutrons made by cosmic rays in large liquid scintillator detectors. Muons from cosmic rays make neutrons as they pass through matter. Those neutrons form a key background for rare event hunts, such as dark matter and double beta decay searches.

They match real neutron yields and counts to sims. The sims use the GEANT4 toolkit with three sets of physics rules. Data from the Daya Bay reactor neutrino work anchor the tests. Sound background models help rare event hunks set true limits.  The yield checks span more than one detector data set.
arxiv-2601-12580:
Sofiya Zaichyk presents a formal framework for coordination among many AI agents with no central boss. The framework is called Semantic Fusion. Agents work over scoped views of a shared memory. Each agent can propose structured updates to that memory. Global coherence must hold even though control is spread out.

The framework keeps coherence through local checks and refresh steps. Checks use a shared ontology, a formal map of concepts and relations. There is no centralized control and no explicit message passing. That design aims for systems that scale without a single point of failure. It speaks to distributed algorithms, temporal logic, and probabilistic computation at once.
arxiv-2601-12680:
Zheng Fang and six co authors work on teaching language models to use tools well. Tool learning lets a model pick and combine external tools for complex real world tasks. With tools, a model goes beyond pure language and can act in specialized ways. The challenge is to make that skill generalize to new tools and tasks.

Their system is called MetaToolAgent, built on meta learning. Meta learning trains a model to adapt fast to fresh problems. Applied to tools, it should let a model learn new tools from few examples. Generalizable tool use is a key step toward agents that work in open settings. The work speaks to the fast growing agent research community.
arxiv-2601-13180:
Shreesha Rao D. S and co-authors take rare lab marks of a special glass fibre. The fibre is made of ZBLAN glass with a small oval core. It keeps the lean of light waves fixed as they pass. Such fibres draw work for light work in the mid infrared band.

Two marks are key to model fast pulse flow in them. One is group birefringence, the split in speed by wave lean. The other is group velocity dispersion, how pulse speed shifts with hue. Lab data for both marks were scarce. The team fills that gap. Their marks help staff who build supercontinuum sources and fast fibre lasers in that band plan with real numbers, not guesses.
arxiv-2601-13380:
Chaoxin Wang and co-authors give hands on guides to semi supervised object detection. The task trains a detector with few marked pics and many unmarked ones. That mix fits fields where marks cost a lot, such as scans or field pics.

Past work in the area grew fast, with many tricks that are hard to sort. The team shares what works in real use and where gains are thin. They weigh how pseudo marks for the unmarked set are made and kept clean. For vision teams with thin mark funds, sound guides can save weeks of blind tests. The piece is a field note set, not a new model claim.
arxiv-2601-13480:
Matthias Y. He and Eric B. Ford build one model to match two marks in the Kepler planet census. Kepler showed that planet sizes split in two crowds. A gap, called the radius valley, parts super Earths from sub Neptunes. Kepler also showed that worlds in one system tend to match in size, a peas in a pod mark.

A good growth model must yield both marks at once. Their model is a hybrid. It joins clumped multi planet forms with orbits set by a stability bound based on angular momentum deficit. By match of both marks, the model ties size growth to orbit calm in one tale.
arxiv-2601-13580:
Ahmad Al-Zuraiqi moves trained transformer layers as organs from one model to a next. His frame is called Neural Organ Transplantation. In stock fine tune, taught weights are tied tight to one model and its train data. They cannot be reused with ease in a next model.

His swap cuts a run of layers from a taught model as a donor organ. That run is taught on its own on field data. It is saved as a lone checkpoint file. It can then be set in a fit host model, with no need for the first train data. For teams that adapt models per field, reusable layer organs cut cost and time.
arxiv-2601-13780:
Antoine Siraudin and Christopher Morris build a faster way to generate new graphs with AI in 2026. Graph diffusion models make state-of-the-art graphs, from molecules to social nets. Their cost grows with the square of the node count. Much of that cost is spent modeling edges that are not there, in sparse graphs.

The pair compress graphs into a low-dimensional latent space first. Diffusion then runs in that small space, not on the full graph. Laplacian autoencoders do the compression and rebuild steps. Latent diffusion has cut costs in images, and may do the same for graphs.
arxiv-2601-13980:
Rishin Madan and co-authors study the geometry of flux surfaces with quasi-poloidal symmetry in 2026. Such magnetic fields aim to confine plasma in fusion devices. Quasi-poloidal fields bring prized traits: no radial drift of guiding centres, and zero Pfirsch-Schlüter current. They also damp poloidal flows less, which can cut anomalous transport.

Lower transport means heat stays in the plasma longer. Possible stability benefits add to the draw of this symmetry. The team examines the shape of the flux surfaces that carry it. Sound geometry is a base step toward stellarators with this design.
arxiv-2601-14180:
Yichao Liu, Zongru Shao, Yueyang Teng, and Junwen Guo denoise low-dose CT scans without paired clean data in 2026. Self-supervised learning has been increasingly investigated for low-dose CT denoising. Paired normal-dose data are often difficult to collect for training. Many blind-spot methods suffer training inefficiencies and suboptimal performance.

Restricted receptive fields limit what those methods can see in a scan. Their progressive J-invariant self-supervised learning targets those flaws. J-invariance keeps the model from cheating by peeking at the pixel it predicts. Cleaner low-dose scans could cut radiation exposure for patients.
arxiv-2601-14480:
Egemen Erbayat and five co-authors set shared ground rules for network design in this 2026 paper. Mobile networks are moving toward 5G and 6G architectures. Passive optical networks offer a critical solution for cost-effective fronthaul transport, the links that carry data from antennas inward. Many optimization strategies compete in this space.

The literature lacks standardized evaluation models, so objective comparison of those strategies is hard. The team proposes a unified benchmarking framework. It standardizes cost catalogs and deployment scenarios for PON-based fronthaul design. Readers get a common yardstick, so future design claims can be checked against the same facts.
arxiv-2601-15080:
Ka Kit Kelvin Ho, Vladislav Yu. Shishkov, and a large team report cooling a quantum fluid with light-like control. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a Bose-Einstein condensate of exciton-polaritons. These hybrid light-matter particles form the condensate far from equilibrium.

The team observes stimulated cooling of that condensate. It falls from near room temperature all the way down to about 20 kelvin in the test. They map the condensate in energy and momentum space. Careful interferometric tests then set the true condensate apart from the hot particles that sit in excited states.
arxiv-2601-15180:
Pedro Ângelo, Atsushi Igarashi, Yuito Murase, and Vasco T. Vasconcelos add staged code generation to a language for message passing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with session types, which state the shape of a conversation between programs. Metaprogramming lets a program write code in stages.

The authors build on contextual modal type theory with multi-level contexts. Contextual values can close a term over a set of variables. Those values can be boxed and sent inside messages. The work shows how staged generation and session-typed messaging can live side by side in one language.
arxiv-2601-15280:
Chloe Qianhui Zhao, Jie Cao, Jionghao Lin, and Kenneth R. Koedinger let an AI tutor give feedback and compare it with a teacher's. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with feedback that is timely, targeted, and multimodal. Such feedback helps students fix errors fast and stay motivated.

Making that feedback at scale is the hard part. The authors build a real-time AI system for it. It joins written explanations with media: the most apt slide page, plus streaming AI audio narration. Their title reports the outcome: learning matched educator feedback, and student perceptions were better.
arxiv-2601-15380:
Elon Litman and Gabe Guo rethink the attention step inside transformer models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how attention weighs the parts of an input. Seen through entropic optimal transport, standard attention solves a transport problem with a hidden assumption.

That assumption is an implicit uniform prior. The authors replace it with a learnable, continuous prior. Their mechanism is called Goat, short for a generalized optimal transport attention with trainable priors. It aims to encode each patch's context better. The design promises attention that adapts to the data instead of treating all routes alike.
arxiv-2601-15680:
M. P. Thejitha, James A. Sellers, and S. N. Fathima count colored partitions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their counting function tracks multicolored partitions of a number. Even parts and odd parts get different color allowances. Even parts may appear in one of r colors. Odd parts may appear in one of s colors. Both r and s are fixed, at least one each.

Parity restrictions drive the paper, per its title. Splitting parts by even and odd is a classic move in partition theory. Adding colors multiplies the structures to count. Such problems often yield generating functions with elegant forms. They also connect to q-series and modular forms. The authors work in that tradition, asking what arithmetic traits the counts display.
arxiv-2601-15780:
Pascal Benschop, Justin Dauwels, and Jan van Gemert test vision-language models on synthetic video in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial reasoning in these models stays fragile. It breaks when meaning hinges on subtle timing or geometry. The authors build a synthetic benchmark to probe two skills. One is situational awareness: telling a harmful interaction from a benign one. The other is spatial awareness: tracking who does what to whom.

Relative positions and motion also fall under the second skill. Synthetic video gives full control over those cues. Each factor can be varied while others stay fixed. That control exposes exactly where models fail. Real video cannot isolate causes so cleanly. For safety uses like monitoring, knowing a model's blind spots is essential.
arxiv-2601-15880:
Dennis Dobler, Alina Schenk, and Matthias Schmid build a regression method for comparing treatments in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their effect measure is the relative treatment effect. It compares outcome variables from two samples. It reads as a probability: how likely one sample's outcome beats the other's. It also links to the area under the ROC curve. The measure has been used for ordinal outcomes and for censored time-to-event data.

Their approach uses pseudo-observations in a two-sample regression. Pseudo-observations let standard regression tools handle the effect. That makes adjusting for covariates more straightforward. Clinicians like probability-scale effects because they are easy to explain. A method that puts such effects into regression form widens their use in trials and studies.
arxiv-2601-15980:
Martina Formichetti and four co-authors infer wall roughness from sparse data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Surface roughness shapes turbulent boundary layers. It acts mainly through the roughness function and the equivalent sand-grain height. Finding that height directly needs detailed velocity and wall-shear data. Such measurements are often impractical in real facilities. Roughness therefore often goes unmeasured where it matters.

The authors build a data-driven framework for the inference. Sparse experimental data go in; rough wall properties come out. The title calls the process assimilating rough features. Wind tunnels, pipelines, and aircraft surfaces all live with roughness effects. A tool that reads roughness from little data helps engineers predict drag and heat transfer without costly full surveys.
arxiv-2601-16680:
Zhenduo Wen and Amin Gohari study how to pack data with a kind of care. A pack tool is stable if small tweaks stay small. Change a few marks in the source, and the code should shift just a bit. Their 2026 preprint sets out this trait and tests known tools. A famed tool, random binning, fails the test flat.

In random binning, near twins can land in far bins. That leap breaks the care trait at once. The authors build the base math for stable packs. Such packs could guard streams where inputs shift by bits. They may also help codes that must shrug off small noise.
arxiv-2601-16880:
Bethan Evans and Jared Tanner work out the least nudge that flips a deep net's call. Small weight shifts can tilt a call in a set aim. Their 2026 preprint finds exact forms for that least shift. One-layer forms fall out in full. The team names what sets the shift's size.
