Expressions of concern alert readers while editors weigh evidence and possible further action. The paper put forward combining ivermectin with checkpoint immunotherapy for breast cancer. No verdict on the findings accompanies this notice. Readers are directed to treat the original results with caution pending resolution.
pmc-13241580: Kinjo's team at Tokyo Women's Medical report a case of adenosine-sensitive focal atrial racing arising years after a Fontan operation. Catheter mapping placed the focus on the crista terminalis, close to the sinus node. Heat ablation ended the racing. The authors caution that later Fontan rework or a Maze operation could miss this focus. They urge ablation for such rhythm faults before any rework is tried.
pmc-13242380:
Faraj and McCutcheon at MD Anderson review how radiosurgery for pituitary adenomas quietly erodes hormone function. Focused beams control leftover or returning tumors well. Hormone calm in secreting tumors, though, can lag years behind surgery. The review weighs how often it strikes, who is at risk, and shielding plans.

Gland failure strikes between a fifth and a half of treated patients. Damage lands on the hypothalamus, gland, or stalk, with axes failing in shifting order. Shortfalls may surface years later, so hormone checks must last for life. Sharper imaging cuts, careful dose tuning, and gland shifting reduce stray exposure.
pmc-13247680:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes issued this 2026 safety opinion in the EFSA Journal on extending the approved uses of a food enzyme. The enzyme, beta-galactosidase, breaks down lactose and is produced by a genetically modified Bacillus licheniformis strain for the company Novozymes. It had already passed safety evaluation for one manufacturing process, and the applicant wanted two more processes covered.

The panel recalculated how much of the enzyme Europeans would eat under all three processes, estimating worst-case exposure in milligrams of total organic solids per kilogram of body weight per day. Combining that exposure estimate with the earlier toxicology evaluation, the panel concluded the enzyme raises no safety concern under the revised conditions of use. Such opinions are the scientific basis on which European regulators approve food enzymes.
pmc-13248780:
Tiglao and Adao hunted for free-living amoebae in tap water in Quezon City, Philippines, reported in 2026. These microbes live widely in water and soil, and some can infect people or shelter harmful bacteria. The pair sampled twenty-six faucets in homes, laboratories, restrooms, and public parks, then identified what grew using shape and DNA sequencing.

Sixteen faucets, about three in five, carried amoebae. Twenty-one isolates were named, most often Vermamoeba vermiformis, with several other genera appearing once each. Two isolates defied identification. Given the high hit rate, the authors urge routine monitoring of city water systems to protect public health.
pmc-13248980:
Hadžić and colleagues reviewed how obesity changes asthma and its newest treatments, in a 2026 narrative review. Fat tissue presses on the lungs mechanically and stirs body-wide inflammation and metabolic trouble, creating a distinct obese asthma pattern. That pattern often responds unevenly to standard care, so the team examined how biologic drugs perform in heavier patients.

Obese patients more often show a neutrophil-heavy inflammation type that many biologics do not target. Results vary by drug, with tezepelumab showing the broadest benefit so far. The authors also note promise in diabetes drugs that aid weight loss, and they call for trials designed around obese patients, including better dosing and marker studies.
pmc-13249780:
Treittinger and co-authors probe how fast mental control adapts when task rules flip, in a 2026 psychology study. In Stroop tasks, where a color word must be named by its ink, interference shrinks when clashes are frequent. Earlier work found adaptation lands quickly in one direction and sluggishly in the other, an asymmetry the team tested with every participant experiencing both switches across four experiments.

Practice effects, from simple speeding to item-specific learning, repeatedly masked or mimicked the asymmetry in the color-word version. A cleaner face-name version, with fresh stimuli for the second switch, showed the lopsided adaptation clearly and in either order. The authors discuss what this stiffness means for theories of mental flexibility.
pmc-13249880:
Zhu and a Chinese team built an artificial eye material that adapts to light like a real retina, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Their device pairs titanium dioxide with a conductive polymer whose electrical behavior shifts as it absorbs or releases water. Heat from incoming light tips that water balance, dimming the device's sensitivity in bright scenes and boosting it in dark ones, with no control circuitry needed.

Arrays of the devices fed a neural network that recognized images under mixed lighting, bright and shadowed in the same frame, with accuracy above ninety-one percent. The authors propose the self-adjusting sensor for self-driving cars and humanoid robots that must see across harsh, uneven light.
pmc-13250380:
Yılmaz and colleagues test whether blood group predicts survival after surgery for early-stage colon cancer. Their 2026 Cancer Management and Research study reviews one hundred fifty-eight patients with stage two or three tumors treated at one center between 2016 and 2024. Blood group antigens can affect cell sticking and inflammation, which motivated the question.

Patients were followed for a median of about two and a half years, and just under one fifth of them died. Those with blood group B lived shorter lives than those with group O, and group B stayed an independent warning sign after other factors were weighed. Other blood groups showed no clear survival difference. The authors propose blood typing as a cheap extra prognostic marker, pending larger prospective checks.
pmc-13250880:
Lewis and co-authors evaluate a guided online therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder inside routine British health care. Their 2026 European Journal of Psychotraumatology study covers Spring PTSD, a digital trauma-focused cognitive behavioral program with brief therapist support. Four hundred sixty adults with a primary PTSD diagnosis supplied outcome data.

Symptoms of PTSD, general distress, daily functioning problems, and subjective distress all fell from start to finish of treatment. Patients who finished rated the program highly, most calling it excellent or good. Large amounts of missing data, gathered through busy therapists, limited how firmly engagement could be judged. The authors back guided digital therapy as workable and scalable, while urging better data routines in real services.
pmc-13251080:
L Skipper and colleagues make the case for patient involvement in Long COVID research in this 2026 paper. Involving patients and the public can make research safer and fairer, yet it often stays tokenistic or missing altogether.

Drawing on their network's reflections and one running trial, the authors show patients acting as collaborators at every stage, from shaping questions to study design and delivery. That input changed how the team handled outreach, access, and participant safety. Flexible and accessible ways of working were key. Although built around Long COVID, the authors say the approach fits other long-term conditions and wider clinical research.
pmc-13251280:
Getachew Mihiret and a large team pool pregnancy weight data in Ethiopia in this 2026 review. How much weight a mother gains in pregnancy shapes her own and her baby's health, but Ethiopian figures had never been combined.

Thirteen studies with 6,099 women gave an average gain of just under ten kilograms. Only about four in ten women gained within the healthy range, while over half gained too little and about eight percent too much. Eating three or more meals a day, animal-source foods, and three or more clinic visits supported healthy gain. Being underweight before pregnancy raised the risk of gaining too little.
pmc-13253980:
Rayan Khalid and Imad Fadl-Elmula report a rare chromosome disorder in a 2026 case report from Sudan. A five-month-old girl had slow growth, unusual facial features, a cataract present at birth, and a hole between the heart's lower chambers. Notably, she lacked the iris defect that gives Cat Eye Syndrome its name.

Gene tests confirmed an extra marker chromosome from chromosome 22, written as 47,XX,+idic(22)(q11.2). The authors call hers the first documented case from Sudan. They say the case widens knowledge of how the syndrome can look and shows the need for gene testing access in African populations.
pmc-13257080:
Ahmed, Getting, Ashioti, and Lange tested whether blocking peptidylarginine deiminase enzymes helps brain cells recover from ischemia-like injury. These enzymes alter proteins and are blamed in central nervous system damage. Human neuron-like and astrocyte cell cultures went through oxygen-glucose deprivation, scratch injury, and bacterial toxin exposure, with pan-enzyme and isozyme-specific blockers applied at several time windows.

The pan-blocker Cl-amidine sped wound closure in both cell types and reduced histone citrullination. It also shifted structural markers and lowered an inflammatory cytokine in astrocytes after deprivation plus toxin. The two cell types carried different main isozymes. The authors argue several family members add to acute injury, making broad blocking appealing.
pmc-13259280:
Martin Xu and co-authors give drone pilots a guide rail instead of taking the controls. Fully automatic inspection flights face rules and risks, while hand flying makes photo coverage patchy. Their 2026 platform overlays planned paths in augmented reality while a pilot keeps manual command.

A second module grades coverage live, flagging redundant views and shaky triangulation geometry. In a building facade trial, guided pilots held planned spacing and stand-off distances far more evenly. The resulting photo sets sampled the surface uniformly, which improves three-dimensional reconstruction quality. Human judgment plus computation, they argue, beats either alone.
pmc-13259580:
Robert Campbell, Devin Sydor, and Chaim Bell comment on where Canada's scarce anesthesiologists should stand during cataract surgery. Their 2026 CMAJ commentary responds to new Ontario research on care models for the operation. A workforce crisis in anesthesiology frames every line.

The study they discuss found modestly fewer emergency visits and complications when an anesthesiologist took part. Yet surgical risk scores were never built for cataract work, the authors note. No preoperative profile reliably shows which patients will truly need an anesthesiologist's hand. Smart deployment, matching specialists to real risk, is their prescription.

pmc-13264580:

pmc-13271480:

pmc-13271880:

pmc-13273780:

pmc-13274880:

pmc-13275580:

pmc-13276280:

pmc-13276580:

pmc-13276780:

pmc-13278580:

pmc-13279580:

pmc-13279880:
