pmc-13406280:
Sunanda Yogi and Amit Singh review how brain cells break down in a 2026 article on diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Each disease has its own signs, yet they share deep faults: proteins fold wrong, cell power units fail, rust-like damage builds and swelling flares. Each one adds its own twist on top.

A layered marker scheme pulls the strands together for earlier spotting of disease and risk. Shared paths across diseases hint that drug mixes hitting more than one target could help more. The pair argue that reading the diseases side by side, not one by one, sharpens both tests and cures. Signals that pass between paths get close attention as a shield for nerve cells.
pmc-13407580:
Xingze Li and co-authors profile, in 2026, the bacteria living around macadamia tree roots, asking whether nut cultivar or tree age shapes that hidden community. Soil came from five major cultivars at five and eight years old, and gene sequencing charted which bacteria lived there and what they likely do.

Two bacterial phyla dominated, Actinobacteria and Chloroflexi, with Rhodoplanes the leading genus. Cultivar proved the strongest driver of group differences, while age mattered in ways that depended on the cultivar. Likely functions centred on processing amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids, matching host needs. Bacteria mostly co-occurred positively in tidy modules, hinting at cooperation. The authors suggest cultivar-aware microbial starters could support yield and quality in macadamia orchards.
pmc-13408680:
Benedikt Kuhn, Peter Kovermann, and colleagues resolve in 2026 a long argument about a membrane protein that seemed to break the rules dividing transporters from channels. The protein, SLC26A11, is abundant in the brain and had been described both ways. Structural imaging, biochemistry, and simulations together settled the question: it truly does both jobs.

By every structural hallmark the protein is a working transporter, and the team identifies it as the long-sought exporter that moves sulfate out of lysosomes, the cell's recycling units. Its transport cycle also opens an uncoupled chloride conductance, switched by the very sulfate transport it accompanies. That dual nature suggests routes toward treating brain swelling, where chloride movement matters, and toward probing lysosomal storage diseases, where sulfate handling goes wrong.
pmc-13409080:
Sumathy Ravi and co-authors build a questionnaire in 2026 with, rather than for, people living with type 2 diabetes in Western Sydney. Clinic visits are short and clinician-led, so patients' own priorities often surface too late or never. Ten patients and eight health professionals, from specialists to pharmacists, shaped the Diabetes Priorities Questionnaire through hybrid focus groups at a hospital service in a disadvantaged, culturally diverse district.

Four conversations structured the design work: what the tool is for, whether it is usable, what good completing it does, and whether it asks the right questions. Draft items went back to participants repeatedly, and their recorded feedback drove successive revisions. The finished tool is meant to be completed before appointments so consultations start from the patient's agenda. The report documents the codesign process other services would need to repeat locally.
pmc-13410580:
Yewon Han and Lee Sael present in 2026 a faster way to spot gene networks that change in colon cancer. Cancer cells rewire how genes act together, not just how much each gene is used. Older network methods capture that rewiring slowly and often miss the full picture.

Their method, shortened to EDLNA, splits gene activity data into hidden patterns for healthy and cancer samples separately. Comparing the two networks flags which gene links changed. Extra checks against protein networks and gene switches then find working modules. On test data the method ran much faster than rivals at similar accuracy. On real colon cancer data it found stage-linked gene groups that simple gene-by-gene scans missed.
pmc-13411280:
Safia Ansari and colleagues review in 2026 cases of a runaway inflammation syndrome, HLH, at an urban hospital serving a vulnerable population. The syndrome mimics sepsis and cancer, which delays its recognition, and adult data from underserved groups are thin. Records spanned 2019 to 2025 at one tertiary center.

Screening 273 flagged patients yielded 68 likely cases, narrowed to 25 after careful review. Seventeen were recognized during their hospital stay, while eight met criteria only in hindsight. Recognized patients were younger and mostly Black or Hispanic, often uninsured. Death struck about half the recognized group and nearly nine in ten unrecognized patients. Specialist consultation reached every recognized case, which hints recognition itself saves lives.
pmc-13411880:
Zenia Taluja leads a team in 2026 stress-testing draft survey questions about phone and internet access with villagers in Uttar Pradesh, India. Measuring the digital gender gap demands questions people actually understand. One hundred one cognitive interviews, more with women than men, walked through 118 Hindi-translated draft items.

Seven problem families surfaced, from wrong word choices and tangled phrasing to alien ideas like online privacy or hacking. Questions about permission to use a phone tangled with ideas of help, since phones get shared. Rating scales and vague time frames confused many respondents. Nearly every question needed revision despite careful translation, which proves the worth of this slow checking step.
pmc-13415880:
Assem F. Alabu-Husain and co-authors introduce a Pray Optimization Algorithm for hard engineering search problems, in 2026. The method mimics steps of Islamic prayer gatherings in three phases: finding a suitable mosque, aligning the congregation, and accumulating a score that drives convergence toward the best solution.

Standard benchmark problems from the CEC2017 suite tested the algorithm against six strong rivals, with statistical tests confirming its edge. Three classic engineering problems followed. Finally the method planned trajectories for a six joint industrial robot arm, beating five current methods there. Ritual inspired search joins the long list of human inspired optimizers.
pmc-13415980:
Shun Aoki and colleagues report a bladder cancer case with an unusually good outcome after surgery alone, in 2026. A woman aged seventy-six came with visible blood in her urine for a month. Scans and cystoscopy found a three centimeter tumor on the bladder's left wall, with no spread to nodes or distant sites.

Tissue examination after initial resection identified primary large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, a bladder cancer type reported fewer than fifty times. This cancer is aggressive and usually treated with surgery plus chemotherapy. Radical bladder removal alone was used here. Long term freedom from recurrence followed, which the authors present as evidence that early curative surgery can sometimes suffice.
pmc-13417980:
Cynthia Schneider and colleagues map what helps or hinders lung cancer screening uptake, in a 2026 scoping review. Low dose scans cut deaths in high risk smokers, yet participation stays low. Studies from 2013 to mid 2025 were sorted with a behaviour framework covering capability, opportunity, and motivation. Thirty nine studies met the criteria.

Awareness of personal risk, belief in screening benefits, and clinician recommendation most often lifted uptake. Misconceptions, competing life priorities, and fear of results most often held people back. Knowing screening helps did not always translate into attending. Programmes should pair clear communication with easier access and support around fear, stigma, and trust.
pmc-13418380:
Elia Tamagnini and colleagues engineer a coronavirus spike protein that can no longer grip its human receptor yet still trains immunity, in a 2026 mouse study. Vaccines use spike to raise antibodies, but spike's grip on the ACE2 receptor has been proposed as a factor in rare side effects. Point changes were designed to break that grip while keeping the protein's shape.

Mutant spikes bound ACE2 poorly in lab tests. In mice they raised immune responses equal to or better than the natural spike and protected animals on challenge. The design offers a template for vaccine antigens stripped of unwanted host interactions.
pmc-13418480:
Huihui Xu and colleagues model whether a new liver cancer drug pairing is worth its cost in China, in a 2026 economic analysis. Finotonlimab plus bevacizumab beat the older drug sorafenib on survival in trials for inoperable liver cancer. Their model extrapolated survival and tallied costs and quality adjusted life years from the health system view.

The pairing added about 1.27 life years and 0.93 quality adjusted years, yet cost about 48,000 dollars more. Cost per quality year came to roughly 52,000 dollars, well above the stated willingness to pay line. Every sensitivity check kept it above the line, with zero chance of cost effectiveness at that threshold.
pmc-13419180:
Robi Cynthia Chacha and Ermias Mergia Terefe audit how medicines are used at a referral hospital in Kenya, scoring practice against World Health Organization yardsticks. Poor medicine use raises costs and feeds drug resistance, a burden felt hardest in lower-income health systems. Their study ran in the outpatient department of Thika Level 5 Hospital.

The team reviewed 600 prescriptions and watched 100 patient visits, then checked the facility itself for readiness. Standard WHO tools covered prescribing habits, the care patients actually received, and the stock and systems behind both. Yardstick scores like these show managers exactly where habits drift from safe practice. The audit gives the hospital a baseline for targeted fixes rather than broad guesses.
pmc-13419280:
Yong and colleagues piloted in 2026 a national digital programme for type 2 diabetes in Brunei Darussalam. Type 2 diabetes needs steady self-management, and hybrid care mixes app-based support with clinician contact. The sixteen-week programme combined remote health coaching, digital lessons, self-monitoring, and messaging, plus scheduled video visits.

Among those with full data, average blood sugar control improved markedly over the sixteen weeks. About two in three participants hit the preset target for lowering HbA1c, a long-term blood sugar measure, and about six in seven lowered it at all. Fasting glucose, body mass index, waist size, cholesterol, and triglycerides all improved significantly. Quality of life scores rose as well. Completion and video visit attendance were high, and most respondents reported satisfaction with the programme.
pmc-13420280:
Charity Kakuru and colleagues measure how often adults with hypertension in central Uganda treat themselves without a prescription, and what drives the habit. Self-medication here meant taking blood pressure drugs in the last 90 days without formal guidance, by the study's own definition. Their survey ran at Masaka Regional Referral Hospital during August and September 2024.

The study enrolled 192 clinic patients with a mean age of 58 years in the reported group, and 143 of them, some 75 percent of the total, were women. A structured questionnaire captured background and clinical traits, and a modified regression method sorted the linked factors. Unsupervised pressure treatment can mask poor control and clash with prescribed plans. Local rates give the clinic a factual base for counseling and refill policies.
pmc-13420480:
Allison Perko and colleagues recount a neck stabbing case where surgeons, exploring the wound of a 23-year-old man bleeding heavily, found no internal carotid artery on the injured side. Being born without that artery is an extremely rare vessel variant. The right common and external carotid branches were found and named during the dissection, yet the internal branch simply was not there.

The left side, checked by imaging, showed the full normal set of carotid branches. Blood had clearly found other routes to the brain across his life, which is why the variant stayed hidden until trauma forced the question. Bleeding control and repair had to proceed without the expected anatomy as a guide. Trauma teams gain a reminder that a missing vessel on exploration may be a birth variant, not an injury effect.
pmc-13420780:
Aoibheann Power and co-authors survey registered dietitians in Ireland about simulation-based education, training that uses role-play or simulated patients to build clinical skills. Their 2026 mixed-methods study combines a questionnaire with interviews to map knowledge, attitudes, and actual use.

The study included 114 dietitians, fifteen of whom were interviewed. Although 78 percent had encountered simulation activities and 85 percent wanted more training, only 14 percent actually used simulation-based education. Greater familiarity went with more positive attitudes, greater motivation, and fewer worries about resources and cost. Years of experience was the only significant predictor of use. Interviews revealed confusion about what counts as simulation, with many using role-play without naming it as such. Barriers included time, educator training, resources, and institutional support, and the authors call for clearer definitions and coordinated training.
pmc-13421080: Lin Meng and colleagues are named in a correction for their study of a grape gene tied to cold tolerance. The notice is a correction only and alters one time point. In the section on a partner gene, the peak in gene activity was first given as one day of cold. The fixed line gives two days instead. The error is logged in the notice alone to guard the version of record, and no other results change.
pmc-13421380:
Ignacio Fuentes leads a thirteen-author team evaluating, in a 2026 paper, two ruthenium-based glowing compounds as stains for lignified plant cell walls under the confocal microscope. Seeing lignin-rich walls matters for plant anatomy, yet a stain must work inside tissue that glows on its own and must coexist with other labels.

Applied to fixed stems of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, both compounds lit up secondary walls, concentrated in water-conducting vessels and supportive fibres. Their pattern matched established lignin staining methods. Pairing with a second stain separated general wall structure from the ruthenium-marked zones, and the team identified a far-red third label that interferes least. Computer modelling of the compounds' structures rounds out the comparison.
pmc-13421780:
Luis Jesús Garza, José Rodrigo Alcántara Dzib and Luis Raúl Miramontes present, in a 2026 case report, a 66-year-old woman whose scans showed two tumours side by side. She had been treated for breast cancer in 2023, so a new adrenal lump beside a kidney mass raised the obvious fear of spread.

Surgeons removed the right kidney. Under the microscope the kidney tumour proved to be a high-grade clear cell renal cancer with sarcomatoid features, small and confined. The adrenal lump, full of fat on imaging, was a pure lipoma — a rare benign fatty tumour — and not metastasis or the more common myelolipoma. The authors use the case to argue for careful imaging-pathology correlation before assuming the worst.
pmc-13422280:
Martin Ågren leads a seven-author team investigating, in a 2026 Swedish study, what wears adult teeth down. Tooth wear blends grinding, scrubbing and acid erosion, and single-factor studies had blamed everything from age and saliva to jaw clenching without settling their relative weight.

Residents of Jönköping aged twenty to eighty received standardised dental examinations and questionnaires covering health, habits and social background. Examiners scored erosive and physical wear separately and combined, while participants reported their own teeth grinding and jaw dysfunction was assessed clinically; saliva flow and buffering were measured too. Multivariate models then weighed each factor's contribution at once. The authors single out self-reported grinding for special attention in the analysis.
pmc-13423080:
Venerito and colleagues pair a weight-loss drug with biologic therapy in this 2026 matched study of obese patients with psoriatic arthritis, a joint-and-skin disease where obesity blunts biologic response. Thirty-one patients starting tirzepatide, a dual-action metabolic drug, alongside a biologic were matched to 62 similar patients starting biologics alone, and outcomes were compared at six months.

The combination group lost body mass index while controls gained slightly, a gap of minus 2.9 versus plus 0.4 points on the index, and their inflammation marker CRP ended significantly lower. Patient-acceptable symptom state on a disease-impact questionnaire was reached by 48 percent of the tirzepatide group against 21 percent of controls, an odds ratio of 3.44 in the matched analysis, and near-clear skin was also more common. Physician-scored joint targets did not separate significantly, a subthreshold pattern the authors read as real but partial benefit.
pmc-13423180:
Vundamati and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the wider health effects of alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to a sugar found in mammal products. The allergy starts with a lone star tick bite, which primes the immune system against the sugar alpha-gal. The review looked past food reactions to surgery and hospital care, screening 729 records and keeping 14 studies.

Kept studies reported severe allergic reactions not only to foods but also to medical products from mammals. Gelatin, some antibodies, and other surgical ingredients triggered anaphylaxis, a dangerous whole-body reaction, in some patients. Blood transfusions also posed a risk in reported cases. Most evidence came from observational studies in the United States, which limits how far results apply elsewhere. The authors urge surgical and emergency teams to ask about tick-related meat allergy before using mammal-based products.
pmc-13423480:
Yu, Lee, and Kim combine generative AI with mechanics in this 2026 study. They design functionally graded metamaterials. These engineered frames change stiffness smoothly from place to place. Interpolation between known designs often breaks connectivity. It strands struts midair. So the team built a latent diffusion process that respects topology from the start. The process adapts the image-generation technique to three-dimensional graph shapes.

Unit cells are encoded as distinct tokens in a squeezed latent space. They are then diffused and decoded. A mechanistic guidance signal steers generation toward asked-for elastic properties. The framework made everything from repeating frames to graded architectures. The graded forms kept smooth mechanical transitions and intact connectivity throughout. The authors present the method as a scalable alternative. It beats both hand interpolation and purely data-driven generators for inverse design. In inverse design, engineers specify targets and receive a printable structure.
pmc-13423880:
Wittrock and a multi-institute team present magnon momentum microscopy. It is a soft X-ray method that directly images magnons. Magnons are the quantized waves of aligned spins in magnetic materials. The method maps them across a two-dimensional momentum map. Short-wavelength magnons matter for future wave-based computing. Yet detecting them has been a long-standing experimental obstacle.

The team applied the method to yttrium iron garnet, a standard magnonic material. They revealed a rich variety of nonlinear magnon interactions, not seen before. The method is sensitive enough to capture these interactions across wide stretches of the dispersion plane at once. It works at nanometer wavelengths with no frequency ceiling. It also adds element specificity plus bulk sensitivity. The authors present it as a versatile platform for studying short-wavelength and nonlinear magnonics.
pmc-13424580:
Sraya Greenberger leads an eleven-author review of fifteen years of childhood eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic allergic inflammation of the gullet, at their centre. Charts covered 138 children diagnosed between 2009 and 2023, tracking how the disease was found, how patchy it is along the gullet, and how treatment evolved.

The average age at diagnosis was about eight years, and three quarters of patients were boys. Vomiting led the symptoms at 39%, then swallowing trouble and food sticking. Visible changes clustered in the lower gullet, yet biopsies told a patchier story. Some segments cleared the diagnostic threshold while others fell below it. Inflamed tissue sometimes hid under a normal-looking surface, especially high in the gullet. The authors draw sampling lessons for diagnosis.
pmc-13424680:
Boyle and colleagues argue that early drug trials in severe lung failure need better yardsticks for success. The syndrome, called ARDS, fills the lungs with fluid and has no proven drug cure. Many past trials may have missed real gains by use of blunt end measures.

Death alone hides gains that fall short of saving life yet still help patients. The team backs a running scale that tracks each patient's state day by day. Such a scale can spot shifts in health path that one fixed date would miss. It can also weigh death and time on life support in one fair frame. Better yardsticks could help small early trials pick drugs worth large tests.
pmc-13426080:
Carlos Diaz-Salazar and colleagues show that human-specific gene copies slow microglial maturation to match drawn-out human brain development in a 2026 study. Brain growth in man runs on a slow clock, and this work ties that slow pace to a gene set found in no beast but man.
pmc-13426380:
Maria Epifania V. Collantes and Mykha Marie B. Tabuzo systematically reviewed stroke linked with methamphetamine use in a 2026 article following PRISMA guidance. Searches covered studies from 2020 to March 2026, with bias judged by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and eight studies, mostly retrospective cohorts, qualified. The review separated ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke and gathered related vessel and heart pathology.

Affected patients were mostly men, younger than non-users, with fewer traditional vascular risk factors and other illnesses. Mapping mechanisms and subtypes helps emergency teams suspect stimulant involvement in strokes occurring at unusually young ages. Eight sets of data is a thin base, yet the same theme runs through all of them, which lends the shared claim some real weight.
pmc-13426480:
Inumaru and colleagues published a 2026 study mapping two breeding forms of a disease-carrying tick. The Asian longhorned tick spreads fevers in Japan and nearby lands. Some of its populations breed with males, while others clone themselves without males. The team checked 1,750 ticks gathered across 23 Japanese prefectures.

The cloning form turned up in every region the team sampled nationwide. The mating form stayed limited to central and western parts of Japan. Neighboring spots sometimes held one form while the next held both together. The team also built a fast DNA test that sorted every tick correctly. Finer local mapping is their next step for fever risk control. The two forms may differ in how they spread fevers to people.
pmc-13426980:
Zewudu Mulatie and colleagues pooled studies on whether warning flags from automated blood analysers can spot blood cancers early. These machines scan blood samples and raise flags when cell patterns look abnormal, hinting at leukaemia, lymphoma, or related marrow diseases.

Across 28 studies, the flags caught about 91 percent of true cancer cases and correctly cleared about 89 percent of healthy samples. Results varied a lot between studies, driven by which flag type and machine brand each lab used. Flags for abnormal lymphocytes or young blast cells performed especially well in the analysis. Mulatie backs the flags as a cheap first screen, above all where lab resources are scarce.
pmc-13427580:
Josephine S. F. Chow leads a very large team behind a 2026 trial on training for home peritoneal dialysis in Australia and New Zealand. In that treatment, patients clean their blood through the belly lining, and infections at the catheter site or inside the belly remain a frequent problem. Whole dialysis centers, rather than single patients, were assigned by chance to a standard teaching program or to usual local training. The program followed international guidelines for both nurse trainers and new patients.

National registries supplied the outcome data, with time to a first dialysis-related infection as the main measure. Researchers also tracked catheter removal, switches to hospital dialysis, deaths, and quality of life. Pragmatic trials run inside routine care are rare in dialysis, so the design itself offers lessons for testing education at scale.
pmc-13427780:
Bakbak and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on surgery for pouches that bulge from the bladder. Such pouches form when urine pressure stays high, often from prostate blockage. The team gathered 44 studies covering 458 men treated since 1975. Approaches ranged from scope work to open, keyhole, and robot surgery.

Three in four men had prostate surgery at the same time as pouch repair. Major complications stayed rare, at about two in a hundred cases overall. Open surgery tended to bring more blood loss and longer hospital stays. Scope repair showed the shortest operating times in the gathered reports. Every approach improved urine flow, so choice should fit each case. Patient fit, pouch size, and surgeon skill should drive the final choice.
pmc-13427980:
Ziqi Liu and colleagues track, in a 2026 study, thinking problems after removal of tumors on the brain's language-dominant side. Meningiomas at the skull base near the temple can be reached by a route under the temporal lobe. The team enrolled 23 right-handed patients with tumors in the petroclival area during mid to late 2024. Thinking tests and resting brain scans ran the day before surgery, one week after, and three months after.

Patients operated on the dominant side, usually the left, dropped sharply on several test scores at one week. Six of ten in that group showed clear decline, while the non-dominant group held steady. Brain scans pointed to a disturbed network involving the cerebellum, the structure at the back of the brain. The title frames the disruption as temporary, an idea the three-month scans were designed to check.
pmc-13429580:
Mingliang Cheng and co-authors show, in a 2026 study, that blasting a magnetic metal with oxygen plasma turns it into a light-powered semiconductor. Bulk photovoltaic materials generate current from light without the layered junctions of normal solar cells, yet they rarely coexist with magnetism. Their starting material, an iron-gallium-tellurium compound, conducted like a metal and ordered magnetically. Oxygen treatment localized its electrons and flipped it to a p-type semiconductor while keeping magnetism above room temperature.

Devices built from the treated material produced strong currents with no applied voltage, across a broad light range. A small magnetic field could tune the output in a straight-line fashion. Using the measured response, the team demonstrated image cleanup and feature separation with about 92 percent recognition accuracy. Self-powered, magnetically rewritable light sensors are the platform promised.
pmc-13432680:
Manar Elnaggar and Amelie Heuer-Jungemann reviewed in 2026 how tying enzymes to built DNA frames changes how fast those enzymes work. DNA craft can fold strands into exact flat and solid shapes. Pinning enzymes to such frames sets their place and count with rare care, which often lifts their pace past free work.

Past guesses for the lift lean on closeness, charge pull, and local acid shifts, yet none fully fits the reads. Shielding from wear helps too, and a held water skin may add more. Chain reactions with mismatched speeds gain little from closeness alone. Outsize enzymes strain the frames as well. The review maps the gaps and points to uses in green chemistry and built cells, with key puzzles still open.
pmc-13434180:
Qiwei Liu and coauthors explain in 2026 how a helper protein moves a vitamin B12 exporter to the right place in the cell. The exporter, ABCD4, needs the helper LMBD1 to reach the lysosome, the cell part that breaks down waste. Faults in either protein cause rare illness tied to B12 use.

Cryo electron images show the pair in three states, with and without cargo. The helper has nine segments that cross the cell film and a tail that grips the exporter. Cell tests show that breaking the grip keeps the exporter from its post. The maps clarify how B12 is held and moved.
pmc-13435980:
Hsu and a large team reappraise in 2026 what to add when an antidepressant alone fails in major depression. The three classic add-on options are lithium, the hormone triiodothyronine, and second-generation antipsychotics, and the team tested how solid the evidence for each really is.

Their review pooled 56 placebo-controlled trials with 13,616 patients and then stress-tested the results for publication bias and for whether enough data exist at all. Antipsychotic add-ons raised response rates, and that result survived every check; four named drugs carried the support. Lithium looked helpful in a standard pooling, but the effect vanished after bias adjustment. The trials also held only a small fraction of the information a firm answer needs. The hormone showed no clear advantage in its six trials.
pmc-13437180:
Seungoh Kim, writing alone in 2026, argues that calling dental sedation sleep hides a real danger. A recent death during implant care under sedation in South Korea, still under inquiry, frames the piece. A sedated patient who looks asleep may in fact slide into deep sedation, with a blocked airway, weak breathing, or lost reflexes that guard the throat.

Sedation use in Korean dentistry rose from 2020 to 2024, mostly in clinics, and stronger drugs and drug mixes are now more common. Deep sedation relaxes the tongue muscles, so soft tissue falls back and narrows the airway. Blood, saliva, and tools in the mouth add risk, and oxygen masks can hide poor breathing from a simple monitor. Kim insists that whoever gives sedation must be able to rescue a patient who sinks deeper than planned, with trained staff and gear at hand.
pmc-13439180:
Mingfei Song and colleagues build a computing space out of smart surfaces and radio waves, describing the system in 2026. Physical neural networks use real materials to compute, which promises speed and low energy use. Chaotic settings scramble signals, though, and exact maths models of them are hard to build. The team let the messy setting itself do the computing, spread across many tunable metasurface panels.

Training ran fully forward, using live radio feedback to estimate gradients instead of a model of the room. The space named handwritten letters and digits with high accuracy in tests. It also sharpened focusing through disordered scattering and located people in the room reliably. The authors frame the setup as a step toward machines that think through their physical surroundings.
pmc-13439380:
Abdul Rehman and colleagues propose a smarter controller for low-carbon combined cooling, heating, and power plants, in a 2026 simulation study. Such plants wring more use from fuel, yet scheduling them across shifting demand, carbon trading tiers, and response programs is complex. Their framework blends deep reinforcement learning, a self-teaching control method, with quantum-inspired search and a digital twin, a live virtual copy of the plant. Physics-informed neural networks inside the twin model heat flows between plant parts.

Simulated summer and winter runs cut greenhouse gas emissions by about forty percent against separate conventional generation. Primary energy use and running costs also fell by wide margins. The quantum-inspired search settled on good schedules far faster than a standard genetic method. Because all loads were synthetic, the authors frame the gains as a proof of scheduling promise awaiting real plant trials.
pmc-13440280:
Ying Zhao and colleagues identify a protein-untagging enzyme that worsens acute kidney injury by freeing a cell-death protein, reporting mouse and cell work in 2026. Sudden kidney injury kills many patients, and death of tubule lining cells drives the damage. The enzyme YOD1 sits mainly in those tubule cells and rises during injury. Mice bred without YOD1 in tubule cells alone suffered far less damage and cell death under two standard injury models, one drug-based and one blood-flow-based.

Protein fishing experiments found Bax, a known killer protein, as YOD1's direct target. YOD1 strips a specific ubiquitin chain from Bax, letting Bax switch on, move to mitochondria, and trigger cell suicide. Cells without Bax ignored YOD1 entirely. The authors propose blocking YOD1 as a candidate strategy for protecting kidneys during acute injury.
pmc-13440680:
Jaimes Parada and colleagues built a validated word bank in 2026 for assessing language in Brazilian Portuguese-speaking toddlers aged eighteen to thirty-six months. They adapted a standard parent-report inventory and sent questionnaires to three judge groups: experienced speech therapists, other speech therapists, and mothers with no clinical training.

Judges rated words for familiarity and for how well a picture can represent them, the two qualities a test word needs for very young children. Only words meeting the average score criteria survived, leaving 146 words. The team organized them by category into the final bank, designed for clinical assessment and therapy in Brazilian settings. They argue that grounding test words in local family culture makes early language evaluation fairer and more sensitive to real delays.
pmc-13440780:
Ratnaparkhi and colleagues presented in 2026 a narrated operative video showing removal of a hemangioblastoma from a young man's cervical spinal cord. The tumor is benign but blood-rich. Such tumors grow slowly yet can crush the cord, cause swelling, or hollow out a fluid cavity. Surgery is the standard cure, and the neck segment is delicate ground.

The patient, aged 26, had worsening weakness and stiffness from a tumor spanning three neck levels, with bleeding, swelling, and a syrinx, a fluid-filled cavity in the cord. The video walks through the operation step by step. It shows the tumor peeled free along its border with the cord, with the main draining vein sealed last to avoid a flood of bleeding. The tumor came out in one piece. Four months later the man's symptoms had improved markedly.
pmc-13441780:
Raimonda Tamulionytė–Skėrė and colleagues review how heat and housing stress erode stallion fertility, sorting strong evidence from guesswork in a 2026 article. Sperm output in stallions is keenly heat-sensitive and seasonally tuned, while climates warm and management intensifies. The review walks the mechanism chain: heat stress, oxidative imbalance, hormone disruption, and the working fitness sperm need to fertilise an egg, which standard semen checks can miss.

Oxidative stress carries the strongest stallion-specific evidence behind it. Cell suicide pathways, mitochondrial failure, epigenetic marks, and fertilisation signalling rest mostly on work in other mammals and remain unproven in horses. A stallion can therefore look normal on routine semen measures while quietly losing breeding power. Housing, cooling, and breeding management hold the firmest support among fixes, ahead of antioxidant pills and molecular markers, which the authors grade as promising but unsettled.
pmc-13442380:
José Luis Fernández-Vázquez and colleagues report gene maps for four blood strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa taken from two large hospitals in Mexico in 2026. Three strains belonged to type ST309 and resisted nearly all drugs. One strain belonged to type ST233 and resisted all drugs tested.

The team read the full DNA of each strain and compared the gene sets side by side. The ST233 strain held the most drug defense genes, among them blaVIM-2, which breaks down strong drugs. ST309 strains shared a guarded block of defense genes, while ST233 held a block much like a known mobile segment. Most harm-linked genes matched across strains, so high drug defense sat beside a broad set of traits that help the germ cause disease.
pmc-13444280:
Hirotaka Hayashi and colleagues report a born vessel link in a 12-year-old girl with moyamoya disease in a 2026 case paper. She had past brain surgery at another hospital to boost blood paths. Sudden weakness hit both arms and her left leg, which brought her in for checks.

Brain MRI showed no fresh stroke scars, and her weakness cleared on its own, so watchful care was picked. Neck vessel scans found the odd link: her right external and internal carotid arteries joined at the C2/3 neck level in a ring, with a thin inner carotid start. Just nine such born links sit in English reports, and none had paired with moyamoya before. The authors flag the pair as a first, with lessons for scan readers.
pmc-13445380:
Yoon-Jai Hwang and colleagues compare three polymers used in mouth care goods, seeking mixes whose thickness matches human saliva and testing how they shift saliva's germ-fighting enzymes, in a 2026 lab study. Thickness shapes how a mouth gel or rinse feels and spreads. Enzyme shifts matter because saliva's own proteins guard teeth and gums.

The team measured thickness across mix strengths and chain lengths, then tested effects on lysozyme, peroxidase, and a paired enzyme system. Seven mixes matched saliva's thickness in the tested range. Each polymer shifted enzyme activity in its own way, by type, strength, and chain length, and most shifts came at strengths far below those in shop goods. Product makers gain a map for safer blends.
pmc-13447080:
Hongyuan Liu and colleagues report a thirty-eight-year-old woman whose brain dermoid cyst, back after surgery a decade earlier, burst on its own, published in 2026 with a review of like cases. Dermoid cysts are rare birth-born pockets lined with skin tissue that swell slowly with shed matter. A burst can scatter that matter through the brain's fluid paths.

She arrived with headache and vomiting, and scans fit a burst recurrent cyst with spread in the fluid. Emergency surgery, helped by a scope, took out a paste-like cyst, yet scattered pearly foci stayed in the grooves and chambers. Six months later blocked fluid flow swelled her brain, and a second scope operation cleared the foci and eased the pressure. Close watching is the lesson.
pmc-13447180:
Yan Sun and colleagues review flu antivirals in 2026, arguing that current drugs share deep weaknesses. Seasonal flu infects about a billion people a year, yet most benefit from treatment only when drugs start within two days of symptoms. Resistance can also arise from a single viral change, leaving high-risk patients with few proven options.

Newer drugs that block a different viral step show that careful redesign can slow resistance, and the review covers one newly approved drug aimed at another viral part. Combining drugs may help, although a large hospital trial found virus gains did not always mean better patient outcomes. For bird flu strain H5N1, stockpiles lean on one drug class with no trial data in people. Wider stockpiles and ready trial networks top the authors' urgent list.
pmc-13447280:
Jing Zhang and colleagues study hybrid vigour in poplar trees through tiny RNA and DNA marks in 2026 work. Crossbred offspring often outgrow both parents, a gain called heterosis. In herbs, small RNAs that guide chemical marks on DNA help shape that gain, yet trees had not been tested for one phased class of such RNAs.

Whole-genome mark maps and small RNA profiles compared high-growth and low-growth hybrids with their parents. About a fifth of marked DNA sites were unique to hybrids, and mark patterns in gene control regions tracked with gene activity in opposite ways across the two hybrids. Thirteen candidate RNAs and seven key genes emerged, tied to nitrogen use and photosynthesis. The findings offer first evidence for this RNA route in tree hybrid vigour.
pmc-13447980:
Masatsune Ogura discusses in 2026 whether cholesterol treatment should chase a final level, a percentage drop, or both. Guidelines abroad increasingly demand both a low target level and at least a halving from baseline for the highest-risk patients. Japanese guidance still centres on the achieved level alone, valuing simplicity for everyday practice, and a real-world study in the same issue tests the dual approach.

That cohort of patients after artery-opening procedures found larger percentage drops tied step by step to lower event risk. Patients meeting both goals, a very low level plus a halving, fared best of all. Ogura notes a tension, since a patient held at a level most doctors call well controlled could still count as undertreated under dual rules. Simplicity for frontline doctors must be weighed against the extra signal.
pmc-13448280:
Araceli and colleagues ran a prospective 2026 study asking whether removing extra tissue around a brain metastasis helps patients live longer. Some metastases grow in an infiltrative pattern, sending cells into nearby brain, while others stay compact. The team tested whether that growth pattern changes survival and whether a wider removal, called supramarginal resection, offsets the added risk.

Araceli enrolled 50 patients between 2022 and 2025 and sampled tissue at the border between tumor and brain in each case. About three quarters of tumors showed infiltrative growth, and wider removal was achieved in about two fifths of operations. Infiltrative tumors carried clearly worse survival and faster return of disease. Wider removal improved both outcomes only in the infiltrative group and gave no measurable gain in compact tumors, which argues for matching surgical extent to tumor growth pattern.
pmc-13448880:
Shawn Gugliandolo and a large team report in 2026 a small imaging study of how dapagliflozin changes glucose handling in the kidney's outer layer. The work re-analyzes a pilot trial in patients with type 2 diabetes and stable coronary disease. Seven patients per group took the drug or placebo for four weeks, with PET scans during an insulin clamp measuring tracer glucose uptake before and after.

Between-group differences after treatment did not reach statistical significance for any uptake measure. Within the drug group, though, peak uptake fell significantly, while placebo values held steady or crept up. The same downward direction appeared across every renal measure in treated patients. The authors present the pattern as a hint that the drug quiets insulin-driven glucose uptake in the kidney cortex, while noting the tiny sample leaves the question open.
pmc-13449180:
Pricila Mullachery and colleagues evaluate in 2026 whether Medicaid waivers changed how often residential addiction programs use medication for opioid use disorder. Section 1115 waivers let states spend federal Medicaid funds in larger residential facilities that the program's old exclusion had placed off limits. Using national treatment episode data, the team compared states that adopted the waiver in different years between 2016 and 2019 against those that had not.

Medication use was low everywhere but climbed from 5 percent of opioid treatment episodes in 2014 to 18 percent in 2019. States adopting in 2016 showed higher odds of medication use in residential settings, an odds ratio of 1.49, relative to comparison states. Later adopter cohorts did not reproduce that pattern, and waiver adoption made no difference in non-residential settings. The authors conclude any benefit may depend on when and how states implemented the policy.
pmc-13449480:
Hannah Jo, Eman Ali, and Catherine Jensen Peña watch in 2026 how mouse mothers reorganize their care across the day when pups face early-life stress through separation. The standard model removes pups for hours daily, and mothers are known to shower pups with extra care at reunion, which some read as compensation. This team recorded home-cage behavior from postnatal day two to sixteen, with separations starting on day ten, sampling before separation, at reunion, and hours later.

Reunion did bring a burst of contact, confirming earlier reports, yet rough handling rose too and the mothers' self-care fell. When the team summed contact across the whole day with a geometric area measure, stressed litters received no more total care than controls. The reunion increase was borrowed from other hours: a reshuffling, not a bonus. The authors say this nuance changes how separation studies should be interpreted.
pmc-13449680:
Kim compares how Korea, the United States, Germany, and Japan run rehabilitation activity services for people with disabilities. The paper asks what Korea should borrow or fix. Adults with disabilities move far less and face more extra illness. Yet planned programs improve fitness and cardiometabolic risk when people can reach them.

Korea is shifting toward a rehabilitation exercise-and-sport model backed by public services and data-driven local platforms. Documents from 2010 to 2025 show the shift. Split leadership and thin local staff and reach still hold the Korean system back against its stated aims in the analysis. All four countries are moving toward whole-person, rights-based models. Those models have local roots, trained staff, and growing digital tools, though their setups differ widely. Kim urges joined-up pathways, stable public funding, and disability-aware training. Kim also urges compatible data and designing services with disabled people and families.
pmc-13449980:
Bhat and co-authors test a blood-derived booster in this 2026 split-mouth randomized trial aimed at speeding orthodontic tooth movement. Sixteen young adults needing first premolar extractions took part. Each received plugs of leukocyte-platelet rich fibrin in both upper extraction sockets. The fibrin is a concentrate from their own blood. One side later received an injected liquid form of the same concentrate. The other side served as control.

Over twelve weeks, canines on the injected side retracted 4.77 millimeters on average against 3.6 millimeters on control sides, a highly significant difference in the trial's analysis. Fluid sampled from the gum crevice explained the gap. The bone-resorption signal RANKL rose on the experimental side, and its brake, OPG, fell. That combination speeds the bone remodeling teeth move through. The authors conclude the sequential fibrin protocol accelerates canine retraction by tilting local bone metabolism toward breakdown.
pmc-13450480:
Siling Chen, Lan Luo, and Fanghua Gong map in 2026 what the world does for the household contacts of people with drug-resistant tuberculosis. Living with a patient means prolonged exposure, and screening and preventive treatment could break transmission, yet practice varies wildly. Their scoping review searched nine databases through November 2025 and gathered twenty-six studies covering how contacts are screened, which preventive regimens are offered, and where programs stumble.

Most studies used a cascade: symptom checks first, imaging when indicated, then laboratory confirmation. Skin or blood tests for latent infection were often layered in. The studies concentrated in high-burden, lower-income countries, notably Pakistan, South Africa, and China, with multicountry work spanning three continents. Child contacts received attention in several studies. The authors organize the patchwork by theme to expose implementation barriers and research gaps, giving guidelines a realistic picture of practice rather than of protocol.
pmc-13450580:
Brunner, Støme, and Kenter examine in this 2026 scoping review a deceptively simple question: how much therapist time do guided digital mental health programs actually consume? Such programs pair apps with human support, and their selling point is saving clinician hours, yet studies count that time inconsistently, often logging only direct messages and calls.

Fifty-four studies published between 2005 and 2026 reported usable figures, and therapists averaged about 215 minutes per patient over programs lasting roughly 10.6 weeks, though the spread ran from 46 minutes to nearly 20 hours. Forty-eight of the studies counted only direct patient contact. A Norwegian case study showed the blind spot: 73.7 percent of patient-related time there happened off the platform, including diagnostic interviews. The authors still find real savings versus face-to-face care but demand fuller time accounting before scaling.
pmc-13451080:
Tacuri Vera and co-authors test in 2026 whether pumpkin seeds can ease worm loads in lambs as drug resistance in farm worms grows. Seed extracts had shown worm-fighting signs in lab dishes, so the team fed whole or ground seeds to lambs with natural infections. They tracked weight, feed intake, worm egg counts, eye color scores, and blood cell shares.

Seed-fed lambs weighed less at the end of the first feed phase, then gained faster once it ended, a catch-up pattern. Egg counts and eye scores did not shift, yet the blood cell share ran higher in seed-fed lambs during feeding. The mixed picture leaves pumpkin seed as a partial aid at best, not a stand-alone cure.
pmc-13452180:
Jin and colleagues explain in this 2026 mouse study how the windpipe gets its width during development, a question with stakes for babies born with narrowed airways. The trachea grows mainly along its length because its lining cells divide in an orderly sideways pattern, and the team suspected a signaling brake called Fstl1 keeps that pattern in line.

Mice lacking Fstl1 grew abnormally wide tracheas with enlarged inner openings. The cause was misoriented division: without the brake, too many lining cells split vertically rather than sideways, widening the tube instead of lengthening it. Fstl1 normally restrains a growth signal called BMP4, and when the researchers dialed BMP4 activity back down in the mutant mice, both the oversized opening and the spindle-angle errors normalized. The work identifies Fstl1 as a sizing control for the developing airway.
pmc-13452280:
Renee Leenen and a very large team follow in 2026, across twenty years, men who never showed up for prostate screening in a European trial. The trial's seven centers let the team split never-attenders from the control arm. Men in the control arm also missed program screening, yet many still took chance tests on their own.

Never-attenders died of prostate cancer at a higher rate than controls. The authors read nonattendance as a mark of low health engagement and distinct habits, which stacks risk past mere lack of screening. They argue that lifting turnout may matter as much as honing the test itself, a point for programs with falling uptake.
pmc-13452380:
Fangzhou He and four co-authors compare how the best runners pace themselves and hold their place in world class 3000 metre steeplechase races. Their 2026 study uses official split times recorded every 100 metres in heats and finals. The runners came from Olympic Games and World Championships held between 2021 and 2025.

The set holds 339 races by 144 athletes, and the team tracked speed, place, and a late race slowing index for each one. Men and women alike ran fast, then slower, then fast again near the finish. The stronger athletes reached a higher top speed and lost less speed late in the race. Which extra marker lined up with success changed with sex and round, so no single pattern fit every race.
pmc-13452580:
Lan and co-authors probe why dialysis so often harms sex life and hormone health. Their 2026 study centres on kisspeptin, a body signal that switches sex hormones on. The team drew blood from sixty-nine people on long-term dialysis and twenty healthy peers of like age. It gauged kisspeptin, plus the brain and sex hormones it should switch on. People with active swelling or primary gland disease were screened out.

Kisspeptin ran about three times as high in the dialysis group as in healthy peers. In women, sex hormone levels stayed low and the brain hormones did not surge as they should. In men, higher kisspeptin went with lower testosterone, the male sex hormone. The link from kisspeptin to weak erections in men ran through that drop in testosterone. The team reads this as a brain response worn down by a non-stop signal.
pmc-13453580:
Yuxin Jin and seven co-authors build tiny glowing dots that let doctors watch T cell killing during heat based cancer therapy. The dots, about 5 nanometres wide, are made from chlorogenic acid, a plant compound, linked with iron. Their 2026 design heats tumors under near infrared light while a surface probe lights up when granzyme B, a killing enzyme from T cells, is active.

The dots kept over 99 percent of their activity after 15 days on the shelf, far outlasting kindred materials. In mice with breast tumors, the heat treatment killed tumor cells in a way that wakes the immune system. The dots also soaked up the excess harmful oxygen species left by heat, sparing the T cells that flooded in. Tumors shrank by 99.42 percent against controls, and the glow let the team tune the heat dose live.
pmc-13454380:
Hernandez-Marquez and colleagues explore how gut cancer patients in Alabama and Mississippi experienced teaching about their surgery. Their 2026 study, part of a larger equity project, drew on interviews with 36 adults treated for colon, esophagus, or pancreas cancers, most of whom had surgery. The team sorted the interview text for things that helped or blocked clear learning before, during, and after the operation.

Patients said clear delivery of instructions helped at every stage, and nurses stood out as the key teachers who explained steps and handed out materials. Barriers were plain: instructions that were incomplete or rushed, most often before and just after surgery. Patients valued explanations in everyday words, not medical terms. The authors argue that fixing gaps stage by stage, and checking what patients grasp, would make surgical teaching fairer and more useful.
pmc-13454480:
Junyao Wu and seven colleagues report, in 2026, that stronger waves can flip where energy piles up inside a specially built material. The effect at play is the non-Hermitian skin effect, where waves crowd against one edge of a sample. Most earlier work used steady, linear materials. The team instead built a microwave structure whose response changes with wave strength.

Under a weak pump signal, waves gathered at one end of the sample. Cranking the pump up moved the pile-up to the opposite end. The structure also produced a third-harmonic signal, a higher tone, whose pattern mirrored the same flip. The team further built a chain model showing two kinds of light-driven phase change. They pitch the effect for switches that reroute waves and for devices that convert frequencies on demand.
pmc-13454680:
Fonseca and co-authors reconstruct the family history of a flowering plant genus split between two great rainforests. Their 2026 paper studies Adenocalymma, a group of lianas native to the Amazon and the Atlantic Forest, which are separated today by a dry diagonal of savanna and scrub. The team sampled 68 species, about 87 percent of the genus, and built evolutionary trees from nuclear genomic data.

All analyses supported the genus as one natural group, with mostly strong support for its internal branches. Gene-tree disagreements owed only a minor share to hybridisation or incomplete lineage sorting. The Atlantic Forest emerged as the ancestral home and the main source of lineages that later populated neighbouring regions, with two clear cases of populations split by barriers. Diversification sped up sharply during the last five million years.
pmc-13455180:
Mangesh Pagadala, Sajid Jalil, Nicholas Dunn, and Ashwani K. Singal review, in 2026, drug care for a liver condition where metabolic harm and alcohol act together. The overlap condition, called MetALD, scars the liver faster than either cause alone. Trials have largely shut such patients out, leaving doctors to borrow evidence from neighboring diseases.

Current care attacks both fronts at once, with alcohol control first when drinking continues. The review surveys liver drugs proven in fatty liver disease, including incretin agents, hormone mimics, and a thyroid-linked drug, for their possible fit here. Some may also curb drinking through brain reward routes. Proven alcohol medicines such as acamprosate and naltrexone, paired with counseling, anchor the other front. The authors close by sketching how dedicated trials for this overlap group should be designed.
pmc-13456580:
Daniel M. Zeitler and four colleagues report, in a 2026 post-market study, outcomes of cochlear implants for adults deaf in one ear. Thirty adults with profound one-sided loss and a healthy other ear received implants at five referral centers. The study tracked speech understanding, hearing with both ears, ringing in the ears, and quality of life over twelve months.

Speech scores in quiet and in noise rose significantly by the one-year mark. Tasks that separate the target voice from a masker improved on both the head-shadow and the two-ear squelch measures. Patients also reported less tinnitus, less listening fatigue, better spatial hearing, and higher quality of life. No comparison group was used, since the design follows real-world approval practice. The authors conclude that implantation is an excellent option for single-sided deafness, with benefits reaching well past test scores.
pmc-13456880:
Fei, Li, and Li examine weekend catch-up sleep and stroke in this 2026 analysis of United States survey data. Many adults sleep less on workdays and repay the debt on weekends, and whether that habit relates to stroke was unclear. The team used national health survey cycles from 2017 to 2023, covering 11,134 adults aged 20 and over who reported weekday and weekend sleep and any stroke history.

Adults who slept longer on weekends than weekdays had lower odds of reporting a stroke. Those who did not catch up had higher odds. The adjusted odds ratio was about 0.78 in the fully adjusted model they fitted. The clearest benefit sat in the two-to-three-hour catch-up group, where odds were roughly forty percent lower. The association was strongest in women, in adults aged 36 to 64, and in people who drank alcohol.
pmc-13457380: Whole-blood TBI point-of-care testing in Level 1 trauma centers — an implementation protocol. Shawn Eagle, Molly McNett, and others write the hybrid protocol. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is an implementation protocol. It plans emergency department rollout of TBI point-of-care testing.
pmc-13458580:

Machine learning software measured 1,275 finger joint images from 124 patients with rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, plus hands from 53 healthy people.

The index tracked clinician swelling scores moderately well, with a correlation of 0.443 across the arthritis patients. It separated swollen from unswollen joints with middling accuracy, and its ability to rule out swelling was notably weak. Values above the healthy cut-offs were clearly linked with swelling, most strongly for the most swollen joints. The tool is not accurate enough for clinic use yet, the authors say.
pmc-13459280:
Elham Babadi and co-authors describe a 21 year old Iranian woman with an unusually large odontoma, a benign lump made of disorganized tooth tissues like enamel and dentin, in her lower jaw. Odontomas are the most common tumors of tooth forming tissue and usually stay small and silent. This complex type stretched from her first molar back to the jaw's ramus and was associated with her second and third molars trapped beneath it. Their 2026 case report describes removing the mass through an incision inside the mouth.

Despite the lesion's size, the surgeons completed the removal intraorally without breaking the jaw or needing any fixation plates or screws. Healing proceeded without complications afterward. At the four month follow up visit, she showed no sign of the lesion returning. Even large mandibular odontomas can be managed through the mouth, the authors argue, sparing patients external incisions.
pmc-13459380:
Yasuhiro Mitani and co-authors surveyed adolescent wind players about playing related pain in the neck, shoulders, and lower back, and how instrument and posture contribute. Their 2026 study questioned 120 members of a high school brass band about pain occurrence, severity, and duration while playing. The team then compared pain patterns between light and heavy instruments. It also compared symmetrical and asymmetrical playing postures, the twisted positions some instruments force on the body during long rehearsals.

Surprisingly, players of light instruments reported low back pain more often than heavy instrument players, possibly because light instruments demand sustained unsupported postures. Students with asymmetrical posture were more likely to report moderate to severe back pain lasting at least three months. Posture coaching may matter more than instrument weight alone, the authors suggest.
pmc-13459780:
Ding Hu and co-authors mapped how the signaling protein NOTCH3 turns ordinary bladder fibroblasts into the muscle like supporters that drive bladder cancer growth. In their 2026 study, the team combined patient derived fibroblasts with bulk, single cell, and spatial gene expression data from bladder tumors. It then silenced NOTCH3 to watch what the fibroblasts lost, tracing the pathway step by step from the initial growth factor signal downward.

NOTCH3 was markedly enriched in tumor fibroblasts across every dataset examined. Silencing it cut matrix deposition, contractile strength, internal oxidant build up, and the fibroblasts' ability to support tumor growth. The chain runs through TGF beta switching the gene on, after which NOTCH3 helps destroy the P62 protein. That disables an antioxidant defense and lets reactive oxygen species build up to lock in the aggressive state.
pmc-13460080:
Binaya Krushna Sahu and co-authors review in 2026 the case for probiotics in keeping the vaginal microbiome healthy. A healthy community is dominated by Lactobacillus species, which hold acidity high and crowd out pathogens. When that balance slips, bacterial vaginosis, yeast infections, and urinary infections become more likely, and pregnancy complications such as preterm labor can follow.

Trial evidence supports certain strains for cutting recurrence of those infections, working through acid production, surface competition, and immune effects. Early work extends to gestational diabetes and anemia in pregnancy. Safety in people with weak immune systems needs care, and strains beyond Lactobacillus are gaining interest. The authors stress that strain, dose, and delivery route must be standardized before routine practice.
pmc-13461480:
Kennedy Diema Konlan leads a Ghanaian team that studied in 2026 why older adults in Sokode, a peri-urban town near Ho, do or do not take their blood pressure medicines reliably. Their community survey covered 202 adults aged sixty and above with hypertension, scoring knowledge on a graded scale and adherence from six behavior questions, alongside personal, medical, and barrier details.

Knowledge was not the problem: four fifths understood their condition and its management well. Adherence still failed for about sixty-one percent. Forgetting, stopping when feeling better, and cultural or religious beliefs each explained roughly half the lapses. Income, very advanced age, and living with the diagnosis for more than a decade each tied significantly to adherence patterns, which the authors use to target support.
pmc-13461580:
Fabiani and colleagues tested in 2026 whether digestate, the leftover slurry from biogas production, can fertilise lettuce without harming the bacteria living on its leaves. Digestate returns nutrients to soil in a circular system, but its effects on leaf microbes and resistance genes were little known. Lettuce grew in a greenhouse under several digestate plans, and the team checked growth, leaf nutrients, faecal bacteria, salmonella, and resistance gene levels.

Fabiani found that splitting the digestate dose across the season gave growth and leaf nutrient levels matching chemical fertiliser. This happened without raising resistance gene counts or faecal indicator bacteria and salmonella on the leaves, even though the starting digestate held some. The fertiliser plan did shift which bacteria lived on the leaves, while total bacterial counts stayed steady. The authors see digestate as workable for lettuce with limited leaf-community impact.
pmc-13461980:
Laura Mickes and co-authors tested whether an eyewitness's confidence means anything in a live showup, the quick one person identification police run when a suspect is caught near a crime scene. Most research uses photographs, where confidence predicts accuracy weakly. In their 2026 work, a laboratory study of 229 participants and a field study of 153 real showup cases from two American jurisdictions both examined live identifications. Response speed in the lab and an evidence strength scale in the field served as checks on correctness.

Confident and fast identifications were more likely correct in the laboratory, and high confidence rejections pointed to innocence. The field cases agreed: witness confidence again tracked accuracy when scored against independent evidence strength. Live showups, long feared as suggestive and unreliable, produced confidence that carried real information in both settings. Run with bias reducing safeguards, the authors argue, showups yield evidence solid enough to keep using.
pmc-13462380:
Lee and La studied in 2026 hikikomori, severe social withdrawal, among young adults in South Korea, and its links to narcissistic vulnerability, a fragile self-image that craves approval. Their survey covered 352 adults aged 19 to 34 years. They measured withdrawal, depression, and the gap between how people experience relationships online versus offline, along two axes: control and affiliation, meaning warmth and closeness.

Lee found depression partly carried the effect: vulnerable narcissism linked to withdrawal in part through raised depression. The strength of that path depended on the online-offline gap in both axes, with the control gap mattering more. In other words, withdrawal tied less to screen time itself than to how different relationships feel across the two worlds. The authors suggest support should target that relational mismatch, not just digital habits, for withdrawn young adults.
pmc-13462580:
Amidu Alhassan leads a 2026 comparative study of sexual violence before age eighteen among women in Ghana, drawing on national health surveys from 2008 and 2022. Laws and policies, including a 2007 domestic violence act, aimed to cut such harm, yet gaps between groups were poorly charted. The team used a World Health Organization equity toolkit to compare rates by age cohort and marital status, .

The national rate fell from over eight percent in 2008 to about six percent in 2022. Never-married women carried the highest rate in both years. Women aged 20 to 24 held the highest estimate in 2008, then fell by 2022. Rates rose in two older groups, women in their late thirties and early forties, hinting at a cohort pattern in who reports harm. Age-based inequality shifted markedly across the period, while marital status gaps stayed modest. The authors call for prevention aimed at the groups still carrying a heavy share.
pmc-13463480:
Al-Essawe and colleagues investigate in this 2026 study why some stallions' semen survives freezing far better than others, a persistent headache for horse breeding. Their suspect is seminal plasma, the fluid surrounding sperm, and specifically whether plasma from good-freezing stallions protects sperm while plasma from poor freezers damages it.

The team cleaned sperm using a single-layer centrifugation technique, then froze samples with no plasma, with their own plasma, or with swapped plasma from the opposite type of stallion. Plasma-free samples kept more intact acrosomes, the cap structure sperm need to fertilize an egg, than samples frozen in their own plasma. Adding plasma from bad freezers pushed more sperm into premature acrosome reactions, while plasma from good freezers preserved the caps. The authors suggest tailoring freezing protocols to each stallion's plasma profile.
pmc-13463880:
Shuailin Li and five co-authors chart the gene activity of two eye surface tissues in healthy people. The cornea bends light and guards the eye front, while the conjunctiva watches for threats and keeps the surface wet. The team lifted cells gently with impression cytology, a press-on collection method, and read both gene messages and their microRNA regulators.

Corneal cells leaned toward barrier strength, tight sealing, and defense against viruses. Conjunctival cells leaned toward immune watch, fluid release, clearing of stray chemicals, and repair. Paired microRNA and gene networks helped explain how each tissue keeps its own role. The map gives eye researchers a healthy baseline for spotting disease changes and new drug targets.
pmc-13463980:
Jiagui Zhong and eight co-authors probe the triangle of depression, poor sleep, and epilepsy in United States adults. The team mined a national health survey from 2013 to 2020, covering 8,223 adults. Depression is common in people with epilepsy, and the pair are known to feed each other.

Adults with depression showed a clearly higher rate of epilepsy in weighted models. Poor sleep carried a large share of that link, accounting for close to half of the total effect in mediation tests. The strength of the link shifted with schooling level and with heart or vessel disease. The authors argue that mood care and sleep care deserve a place in epilepsy prevention plans.
pmc-13464880:
Karaja and colleagues reported in 2026 a three-year-old Syrian girl whose bulging left eye came from a large arachnoid cyst inside the eye socket. Only 18 such cases had ever been published, just five of them in children. The team reviewed them all alongside their patient. She also had a drooping eyelid from birth.

Remarkably, the girl's vision tested a perfect 20/20. Her optic disc looked normal despite the cyst's size, though she had eye pain and visible protrusion. CT and MRI scans together pinned down the diagnosis and excluded look-alike conditions. Surgeons removed the cyst, and the protrusion resolved completely. Follow-up imaging showed no return. The authors argue a large, symptomatic cyst deserves surgery even when eyesight is intact. Pressure can quietly damage the optic nerve.
pmc-13464980:
Şahin Doğan and colleagues report a 2026 study making silver nanoparticles with the leaf extract of Lotus sanguineus, an endemic plant. Plant extracts can reduce silver into nanoparticles without harsh chemicals, a greener synthesis. The particles were tested for breaking down dye pollutants under light, killing bacteria, and stopping biofilms, with computer docking against bacterial quorum-sensing proteins, the signals bacteria use to coordinate.

The particles showed strong dye degradation and clear antibacterial and antibiofilm action in the tests. Docking suggested plausible binding to the coordination proteins that biofilms depend on, a mechanistic hint for the lab results.  A plant-based route that keeps performance while cutting chemical waste speaks to both water treatment and medical uses, pending safety checks on the particles themselves.
pmc-13465280:
Jai-Sing Yang and five co-authors show how a small RNA, microRNA-34a, drives fat buildup in liver cells by muting a master switch. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolism is now the world's commonest chronic liver problem. In liver cells flooded with fatty acids, the small RNA climbed sharply.
