Feeding those parcels to astrocytes shifted the astrocytes toward inflammation, movement, and RNA processing programs, and away from supporting neurons and calcium balance. One cargo change mattered most: less of the RNA for a brake protein let the master inflammatory switch NF-kappaB fire more freely, raising cytokine release. Restoring the brake protein inside astrocytes blunted that response.
pmc-13578180:
Jianye Yuan and co-authors present a 2026 study of how uneven gene activity is inside lung tumors. Working with non-small cell lung cancer, the most common form of the disease, they ask whether genes that stay steady across a tumor can help predict who gains from immune therapy.

The team mapped that unevenness with single-cell data from many tumor regions, then used six machine learning methods to build a six-gene score. Tumors with low scores held more immune cells and more active immune pathways. Two score genes get close study in lab tests, one linked to weaker anti-tumor defense and one to scar-like tissue around tumors. The score may help doctors pick patients for immune drugs.
pmc-13579880:
Hongzi Zhu and colleagues report a rare yeast infection that took hold in a leg wound of a healthy 67 year old woman, in a 2026 case report. The yeast, Trichosporon asahii, usually strikes people with weak immune defenses, yet her system was sound. After surgery to clean and stitch a lower leg injury, her skin died back in patches, oozed pus, and tunneled into pockets, while blood inflammation signs stayed oddly normal.

Three lab methods agreed on the yeast's identity, and drug tests showed it yielded to voriconazole. Three weeks of repeat cleaning surgery, vacuum drainage, and the drug brought the wound under control and started healing, after which the drug was stopped. The authors flag the mismatch between fierce local damage and quiet blood tests as the tell for this invader.
pmc-13582380:
Kim B Kuchemüller and colleagues build a math model of virus making in human kidney cells and plug it into a live monitoring frame, in a 2026 study. The model tracks living, dead, and burst cells against food use, waste buildup, and virus specific harm. First tuned on adenovirus cultures, it was then refitted to two other gene therapy virus types with only small parameter changes.

A sensor layer reading the broth's electric behavior fed live cell counts into the model as it ran, a setup the team calls a digital shadow. In perfusion runs the shadow tracked real cell counts closely and called growth and infection timing on the fly. The authors pitch the pairing as a step toward a full digital twin that can steer virus factories.
pmc-13584280:
Daan Langeveld and colleagues put a whole body of trial reports under a microscope in this 2026 integrity study. The reports are 223 randomized controlled trials, the gold standard design for testing treatments, all tied to groups built around one researcher. The team suspected that the numbers in those trials looked too tidy, with too little of the random scatter that real sampling should leave behind.

Their checks compared starting traits and dropout counts in those trials against 103 trials from other groups on like topics. Dropout numbers came out even far more often than chance allows, and equal dropout across trial arms was three to four times more likely than in the comparison set. The pattern was strongest when the key researcher led the author list. The team questions the worth of those trials.
pmc-13584480:
Nassirou Ibrahim and a large team audit teen health services in Niger in this 2026 study. Teenagers need care for sexual and reproductive health and for mental health, yet in poor settings both can be patchy and wasteful. The team surveyed 160 public health sites in the capital region of Niamey and in Maradi, checking what was on offer and how well each site used its resources.

Nine in ten sites offered sexual and reproductive care to teens, but only one in ten offered any mental health support. On a standard efficiency scale, sites averaged a score near 45 percent, which leaves wide room to do better with the same inputs. The authors call for training staff to handle teen mental illness and for stocked pharmacies that carry the products teens need.
pmc-13585980:
Derya Okuyan and colleagues untangle two signals that switch on an invasion gene in prostate cancer cells. The gene, MMP14, makes the only membrane-bound collagen cutter in its family, a tool tumors use to chew through tissue. Working with PC3 prostate cancer cells, the team varied two inputs: a growth signal called TGF-beta and low oxygen, mimicked with a chemical stand-in.

Low oxygen proved the stronger driver, lifting the gene's output and protein levels on its own and with the growth signal added. Tests with trimmed copies of the gene's control region showed the full-length version answered every treatment, while short versions fell quiet under the growth signal alone. A partner collagen gene moved the opposite way. The picture is of oxygen stress running the show, with TGF-beta playing a tangled supporting part.
pmc-13595180:
Ahmad Subahi and colleagues surveyed radiography interns and recent graduates from two Saudi universities about how well their training built the skills needed for safe practice. Sixty-one respondents came from the 2020 to 2023 cohorts. They rated their perceived growth, course coverage, and confidence. They also rated the value of clinical placements across seven areas of professional competence.

Ratings ran positive for communication, procedural and technical knowledge, patient care, and teamwork, and respondents saw those areas as important for their future work. Two areas lagged on every measure: medico-legal and ethical knowledge, and spotting significant findings on images, arguably the two where mistakes carry the heaviest consequences. The authors offer the pattern as a map for curriculum repair, noting the study rests on self-perception from a small group rather than tested ability.
pmc-13595480:
Anouk E C Bruijnzeels and colleagues followed colorectal cancer survivors for two years to test whether inflammation tracks the many faces of cancer fatigue. Within a population-based Dutch study, 411 newly diagnosed patients gave blood and answered fatigue questionnaires at diagnosis, one year, and two years, alongside a matched comparison group without cancer.

Eleven inflammation markers were measured. The soluble TNF receptors related most consistently to nearly every fatigue dimension. Those receptors are signals tied to a master inflammatory switch. The dimensions covered general, physical, and mental fatigue, plus reduced activity and motivation. Other markers joined in for specific dimensions, and mental fatigue showed the steadiest pattern. Survivors displayed a broader inflammation-fatigue web than the comparison group. The authors see inflammation as a plausible lever for easing survivorship fatigue, with the TNF pathway first in line.
pmc-13598680:
Jeremy B Ducharme and co-authors asked whether pancreatic cancer scrambles the daily clocks of the breathing muscles and heart, extending the known circadian damage of cancer wasting beyond the limb muscles. Using a mouse model that grows pancreatic tumors in place, the team collected diaphragm and heart tissue every four hours across a full day at the onset of wasting.

Roughly sixty percent of rhythmic genes lost their rhythm in both tissues. In the diaphragm, core clock components faded and metabolic programs broke down in step with rest-phase timing, while inflammatory networks gained rhythm and peaked during rest. Heart disruption centered on networks for cardiac signaling, insulin response, and nerve-related genes, with a smaller inflammatory gain. The authors argue that clock collapse in the muscles that breathe and pump may help explain why cachexia kills, and they map the damage tissue by tissue.
pmc-13600280:
Mychal Beebe and Ankur Tayal report a 2026 case of chiropractic care for a man whose neck artery had been partly torn in a car crash. The 54-year-old arrived with severe neck pain, headaches, and a stiff neck, eight months after the crash damaged his left internal carotid artery. Because hands-on neck treatment after an artery injury raises safety questions, the clinicians first reviewed his history, examination, and imaging to judge the risk acceptable.

Over six months he received five adjustments with the Blair upper cervical method, aimed at the top neck vertebra, whose alignment with the skull looked altered. Pain ratings, a neck disability questionnaire, and a general health survey all improved over the treatment period. Beebe and Tayal stop short of firm claims from a single case. They call for more research on whether this care is safe and useful after traumatic artery injury.
pmc-13608480:
Hari Pankaj Vanam leads a six-author team through two puzzling fungus cases from car crash wounds in the Emirates. Crash wounds often carry soil fungi, and a fungus in a culture dish does not prove infection. Worse, some isolates refuse to form spores, defeating shape-based identification and routine mass spectrometry. Reference laboratory sequencing rescued both identifications.

The first patient, a 55-year-old man with a crushed, degloved hand, grew a sterile mold that sequencing named Subramaniula asteroides. No invasion test was done, no antifungal given, and the wound healed with surgery and antibiotics. The second, a 40-year-old man with severe arm trauma, grew Aspergillus quadrilineatus, identified across three gene regions. Doctors started voriconazole, then stopped after fifteen days, judging colonization likelier than infection. The authors argue for molecular identification of stubborn molds, and for restraint in treating what may only be passing contamination.
pmc-13608980:
Levent Deniz leads an eight-author team checking whether white blood cell mix mirrors neck artery narrowing. Monocytes come in classical, intermediate, and non-classical flavors, each playing a part in plaque growth. The team studied 73 adults who had carotid ultrasound, splitting them at 50 percent narrowing of the internal carotid artery. Monocyte subsets were profiled by flow cytometry with inflammation markers and artery wall thickness.

Patients with significant narrowing carried more classical monocytes and fewer non-classical ones, plus higher white cell and neutrophil counts, fibrinogen, and HbA1c. Non-classical share also fell as artery wall thickness rose. Adjusted for age, sex, and blood pressure, a lower non-classical percentage still tracked narrowing. Adding fibrinogen, neutrophils, and HbA1c erased that link, while fibrinogen stayed significant. The monocyte pattern is part of the broader inflammatory state accompanying advanced carotid disease, the authors conclude, not a standalone signal.
pmc-13612180:
Maylis Douine leads a sixteen-author team surveying people who mine gold illegally in French Guiana's Amazon forests. Most are migrants from Brazil's poorest states, living without legal status far from services. The survey enrolled 480 adults at supply bases on the Suriname and Brazil borders in late 2024. It asked about work, health, violence, food, safety, and care access, then clustered answers into profiles.

Hardship was layered. Over half, 55.7 percent, rated their health medium or poor, and 43.9 percent lived over a day's travel from the nearest health facility. About 44 percent felt unsafe, 29.8 percent had faced violence, and 16.7 percent had no social support. One in five experienced moderate hunger, and 21.9 percent screened at elevated mental-health vulnerability. Food insecurity tied to isolation and money trouble; mental vulnerability to being female, isolated, or feeling unsafe. The authors call for harm-reduction work and cross-border public health for this hidden population.
pmc-13613580:
Dequan Zhu and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a 73-year-old woman with two rare problems at once. She had a double aortic arch, a birth defect where the main artery forms a ring of two arches. She also had a dangerous bleed within the wall of her rising aorta, with a small tear inside it. She arrived with burning pain in her throat and upper chest, and doctors first suspected a heart attack.

Scans showed the double arch and how her neck and arm arteries branched from each side. Surgeons opened her chest in an emergency operation and found a tear about two centimetres long. The team reflects on how they planned the repair around the unusual anatomy, since no agreed playbook exists for this pairing. The case may guide other surgeons who meet the same rare mix.
pmc-13613680:
Sumaya Mehelay leads a large team presenting a 2026 framework meant to help health care groups build real equity into their daily work, not just state it as a goal. Recent pushes for equity, diversity, and inclusion grew after the pandemic laid bare deep unfairness and racism in health systems. The authors asked whether such efforts reach the roots of the problem, and set out to build guidance that does.

Their group mixed people with lived experience of structural unfairness with clinicians, scholars, and health leaders, and they drew on a rapid scan of earlier frameworks. The result is a practical frame for shifting power: changing who decides, whose voice counts, and how policies are written. Health groups can use it to test whether their equity work changes systems or only adds surface programs.
pmc-13614180:
Ana González-Ruiz leads a team testing whether human hair can track long-term contact with endocrine-disrupting chemicals, substances that interfere with hormones and are tied to chronic disease. Blood and urine are the usual test materials, yet both capture only recent contact because the body clears these chemicals fast. Hair grows slowly and may hold a longer record. The team built a method covering 44 such chemicals from five families.

Their lab routine combined exact measurement with a wider screen for related breakdown products, checked in paired hair, blood, and urine samples from 20 people after menopause. Comparing the three materials shows what hair adds and where it falls short. A hair-based record could help health studies link years of low-level contact with later illness, rather than relying on a single day's urine test.
pmc-13614980:
Agnieszka Sabiniewicz, Nadine Brühl, Antje Haehner, and Thomas Hummel present a 2026 update of the labels used in the Sniffin' Sticks smell test. In this widely used check, people name odours from a set of answer labels. Labels age with culture: an odour name familiar thirty years ago may puzzle people today, skewing scores. The team tested 83 people with a normal sense of smell, aged 18 to 75, across four studies.

They swapped unfamiliar labels for familiar ones and balanced how often each answer appears, changing 31 percent of the labels in the set. Forty more volunteers then retook the new version after a gap of days to check its stability. Fairer labels mean a low score is more likely to reflect a weak nose, not a dated word list.
pmc-13615080:
T. Hirsch, U. Moser, A. Wolf, and A. Andrianakis report a 2026 pilot study on whether a biologic drug for chronic sinus disease changes the microbes living in the nose and sinuses. Eight patients with long-term sinus inflammation and nasal polyps received dupilumab, 300 milligrams every two weeks, for six months. Nose swabs from the middle passage were taken before treatment and at the end.

The mix of microbes barely moved: variety measures, overall community shape, and single species counts showed no clear change, apart from small, uncertain dips. Clinical results told a different story, with all patients improving markedly over the same six months. The drug seems to calm the disease without disturbing the local microbes, a reassuring early sign, though eight patients is a small base for firm claims.
pmc-13615480:
J. Kurwinkel and colleagues describe four dogs with unexplained lumpy inflammation around the eye, a condition with no found cause and no germs in the tissue. The dogs, a German Shepherd, a mixed breed, a Magyar Vizsla, and a Hovawart, were all female and aged from 1.5 to 5 years. Lumps, ulcerated in one case, sat on the skin near the eye in three dogs, at the inner eye corner in two, and on the third eyelid in one.

Tissue samples showed a mixed pus-and-granuloma pattern in three dogs and a pure granuloma pattern in one, with no sign of infection. All received steroid treatment, three also got cyclosporin by mouth, and one had a lump trimmed before drug care, later growing a new swelling. The report helps vets recognise this odd condition and set owner expectations for a slow, drug-led recovery.
pmc-13615980:
René H. M. Raeven and colleagues compare in 2026 the immune response to a third MMR vaccine dose against the response to a natural mumps infection in young adults. People vary widely in how strongly they answer a vaccine, and spotting weak responders early matters for protecting them. The team used a many-parameter analysis of blood and immune cells after the third measles, mumps, and rubella shot.

The booster raised antibodies, antibody-making B cells, and helper T cells against mumps. Real infection produced the same kinds of response, only stronger, and added a robust killer T cell response the shot lacked. High-dimensional cell profiling also split people into low and high responder groups with distinct patterns, and certain memory T cells tracked with a strong booster answer. Such markers could guide extra doses to those who need them.
pmc-13618180:
Alexander Muacevic and five colleagues compare two heat-based treatments that destroy early liver cancer from inside: microwave ablation and radiofrequency ablation. Both aim to cure, yet which serves patients better has stayed unsettled. The team searched five databases through March 2026 and graded confidence in each outcome using the GRADE framework.

Thirty-eight studies with eight thousand three hundred forty-seven patients, including seven randomized trials, entered the analysis. Initial complete tumor destruction was essentially identical between the two. Microwave treatment, however, carried about a third lower risk of tumor progression at the treated site overall, and nearly half the risk within the randomized trials alone. Survival, distant recurrence inside the liver, complications, and procedure deaths showed no conclusive differences. The authors advise choosing by tumor location, margin goals, safety, operator experience, available technology, and cost.
pmc-13618380:
Ghazala Shahzad and six colleagues present a case where a liver scan finding, the hot spot sign, pointed back to a blocked vein in the chest. Their sixty-year-old patient arrived with facial and arm swelling, breathlessness, cough, weight loss, and bulging chest wall veins. It was the classic picture of superior vena cava syndrome, where the great vein draining the upper body is obstructed. Contrast CT found a mass above the lung root invading that vein.

The same scan showed a brightly enhancing wedge in one liver segment, the hot spot sign, caused by collateral blood rerouting through an alternate vein into the liver's portal system. Bronchoscopy and biopsy confirmed lung adenocarcinoma as the underlying cancer. The authors warn that this pseudo-lesion can be mistaken for metastatic spread, leading to unnecessary liver biopsy, and that recognizing it speeds diagnosis and treatment of the real obstruction.
pmc-13621480:
Joanna Zielińska and four colleagues reviewed immunotherapy for sesame allergy, a food allergy known for severe reactions and rarely fading on its own. Avoidance is today's only defense, so researchers have begun feeding patients tiny, rising doses to retrain the immune system. The reviewers gathered every study of sesame immunotherapy in diagnosed patients through August 2025 and graded its quality.

Nine studies qualified, mostly small cohorts and case series rather than trials. Oral therapy with sesame alone desensitized most patients, with success rates roughly between eighty-five and ninety-seven percent across varied protocols and ages. Lasting tolerance after stopping was documented in only a few, mainly children's, groups. Side effects were mostly mild or moderate, severe reactions needing adrenaline stayed uncommon, and no deaths occurred. Adding an antibody drug helped high-risk adults tolerate treatment. The authors call the results promising yet preliminary, asking for proper randomized trials.
pmc-13623280:
Emily Newton-Hoe and four co-authors interview doctors about how abortion bans in the United States reshape the workforce that provides early pregnancy care. After the 2022 Dobbs ruling, many states imposed total or near-total bans. The team wanted the view from inside clinics, across the specialties that handle early pregnancy.

Between May 2024 and May 2026, the researchers interviewed fifty-five physicians in fourteen ban states: obstetrician-gynaecologists, emergency doctors, and family physicians. Doctors described legal uncertainty narrowing what they dared to do, with care pushed toward specialists. Many felt their duties to patients clash with risks to themselves, and values such as patient autonomy came under strain. Training suffered, through lost skills, harder recruitment, and trainees leaving school less ready for independent work. Burnout appeared both as a result and as a driver of career choices. The authors warn that bans reach beyond abortion.
pmc-13623380:
Carolina Reis Bonizzio and colleagues describe an advanced training course that taught Brazilian colorectal surgery residents on realistic models: synthetic simulators, animal tissue, and fresh cadavers. Hands-on practice in a safe setting is prized in surgical training, since first attempts on real patients carry risk. The course joined online theory with two days of supervised operating practice.

Fifty-two first-year residents from across Brazil took part. Knowledge scores rose after the online phase and rose again after the practical days. Confidence climbed sharply for key operations, including removing the right or left colon through small incisions and a delicate rectal procedure. Residents rated the course above nine out of ten for satisfaction. The authors conclude that the mixed format is practical in their setting and argue for wider use of simulation in early surgical training.
pmc-13623480:
Ulla Palotie leads a very large author group in a 2026 perspective on remaking dental education for a digital age. Artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and touch-based simulators are entering dental schools fast, while the classic phantom head and clinic teaching still anchor training. The authors argue that the mix, not replacement, is the goal.

Evidence gathered since the COVID years suggests that immersive and blended teaching can raise motivation, deepen learning, and even support student well-being when it is woven into the curriculum with care. Digital tools also cut the material waste of traditional practice, which fits global sustainability goals. Access, though, is uneven between schools and countries, risking a readiness gap among graduates. The authors point to international networks that share simulators and benchmarks as a way to spread the gains, and they frame the end goal as safer, more patient-centred care.
pmc-13623780:
Océane A Dubois and colleagues review how machine learning and computer modelling can expose the ways diffuse midline glioma resists treatment. This brain tumour, arising in children and young adults along the brain's midline, is driven by changes to histone proteins that scramble gene control. Nearly every case resists therapy, helped by wide variety among its cells.

The review organises the computing tools around four questions: how the cell mix shifts under treatment, how cell states remodel, how flexibly cells switch identity, and how cells signal to their neighbours. Applied to single-cell and spatial gene data, these methods can pick out stubborn cell groups, replay the paths cells take as they adapt, and chart contacts with the tissue around the tumour. The authors expect that as data sets grow richer, such models will surface drug targets and markers that support treatment matched to each patient.
pmc-13625280:
Heng-Min Xu and nine colleagues, publishing in 2026, ask whether the body's cumulative stress wear predicts death in the UK Biobank. Their wear score, allostatic load, blends twelve measures across heart, metabolic, immune, and kidney systems for adults aged forty to sixty-nine. Over a median follow-up past fifteen years, the cohort recorded 39,804 deaths, led by cancer and cardiovascular causes.

Risk climbed step by step with the score for every cause studied. Each added point raised the hazard most for digestive and heart deaths, and the link ran stronger in people who died before seventy or who joined the study young. A single score built from routine measures, the authors argue, can flag bodies worn down early by stress.
pmc-13626480:
Su Jin Kang and co-authors turn the fat droplets shed by fighter immune cells into bridges between killer cells and breast tumors. Natural killer cells often fail against solid tumors because the tumor neighborhood suppresses them and contact is fleeting. The team's vesicles come from M1 macrophages, the inflammatory kind, and carry two grips. Hyaluronic acid latches a marker on killer cells. A ring peptide grabs tumor integrins. One particle thus holds both sides at once.

In dish and animal studies the bridged killer cells clustered at tumors, woke up, and killed far more cancer cells. The vesicles also spilled inflammatory signals that flipped the tumor neighborhood from suppressive to hostile. Dual gripping plus reprogramming, the authors argue, answers two reasons cell therapy fails at once.
pmc-13629280:
Lee and colleagues solve a wiring problem for transistors built from molybdenum disulfide, a one molecule thick sheet. Such sheets promise low power logic. But pumping extra electrons into set spots, called doping, usually wrecks the crystal or resists control. Their 2026 process runs ammonia plasma over the sheet while a two layer barrier shields it. Damage stops at the barrier. Nitrogen hydrogen radicals slip through and dope the sheet beneath.

The doping reached heavy, degenerate levels while the crystal stayed intact. Computer modeling pinned the effect on NH2 radicals on the surface donating electrons. A second radical type healed sulfur gaps in the lattice. Devices gained sixfold in speed and on current with no shift in switching threshold. Activating the extension regions, the stretches beside the contacts, then cut series resistance sharply. On current leapt by a factor of 260 in tests, with off behavior kept.
pmc-13629980:
Sameera Sharma and thirty-five colleagues, with the ViSON collaborators, lay out a plan for a breath test for one cancer. The target is oesophageal squamous cell cancer. This form drives most of the world's deaths from oesophageal cancer. In Britain most cases surface late, when survival is poor. A breath-based shortcut could send the right patients to endoscopy sooner.

The study will recruit 518 people across NHS hospitals. Half will have the cancer. Half will be cancer-free controls. Breath samples travel on sorbent tubes to a central lab for chemical analysis. A prediction model will be built from the breath compounds. It will be checked for accuracy, calibration, and clinical usefulness. The design targets high sensitivity with solid specificity.
pmc-13631280:
Marco Ruscone and two colleagues show that an AI agent can assemble a working cancer model by chatting with specialist software. Their study appeared in 2026. Building such models, which connect gene networks to cell behaviour to tissue, normally demands coding skill. Several tools must be handled at once.

The agent worked through a standard connection protocol to three platforms. One drew gene regulatory networks. One simulated cell fate logic. One ran multicellular simulations. The result was a model of how cancer cells respond to an immune signalling molecule. It was built entirely through natural language instructions. No hand-written code or manual file edits were needed. The authors extract design lessons about tool sizing and session handling. They warn that results varied by language model and need rigorous checking.
pmc-13631480:
Min examines in 2026, in Korean with an English abstract, how ordinary people in Han dynasty China actually got medical care. Skilled physicians had separated from shamans by the early Han, but their services did not reach far down society.

Drawing on historical records, Min shows that excellent physicians mostly treated rulers, high officials, and their circles. Famous healers from the provinces were pulled toward the capital Chang'an or regional centers by generous pay. Commoners therefore relied on folk healers who doubled as shamans and priests while treating everyday illness with acupuncture and herbs. The state sent court or local physicians to the public only in special circumstances such as epidemics. Herb suppliers to this civilian market, from shaman-doctors and recluses to anonymous gatherers, provided roughly 130 kinds of herbal medicine.
pmc-13631880:
Parasuraman Ganeshkumar and a large team of colleagues published this 2026 survey of high blood pressure care in India. They compared community surveys from 2018 and from 2023 to 2024 in nine districts covered by a national control program. Adults aged eighteen to sixty-nine were sampled in clusters. The team tracked three steps: knowing one has hypertension, receiving treatment, and keeping blood pressure controlled.

In the later survey, more than seven thousand people had hypertension. Well over half knew their condition, under half were being treated, and about one in five had it controlled. Each step had improved since 2018, with control gaining the most ground. Older adults improved more than younger ones across all three steps. The authors say repeated community surveys can show whether such programs truly raise control, a lesson for other low and middle income settings.
pmc-13632080:
Kelvin Supriami and nine colleagues published this 2026 study of how artery disease shows up in different parts of the body. Clogged arteries can strike the heart, the brain's vessels, or the legs, and patients differ in which site is hit first. The team analyzed nearly four hundred seventy thousand UK Biobank participants who began free of such disease. They tracked social, clinical, lifestyle, and genetic influences over about thirteen years.

Each vessel territory had its own risk profile. Leg artery disease tied most strongly to inflammation, blood sugar problems, and smoking. Heart artery disease tied more to cholesterol and to inherited genetic scores. Brain vessel disease mixed both patterns and added a link to social deprivation. Healthy sleep and activity protected against all three. Leg disease most often led onward to disease in several territories and to death, which makes its early risk signs especially important.
pmc-13632680:
Qi Li and five colleagues reviewed stroboscopic visual training, a sports method where athletes practice while their vision is repeatedly blocked for short moments. Special glasses or lighting create the flicker effect. The idea is that training with less visual information forces faster, smarter use of what the eyes do catch. The team gathered studies on perception, thinking, and sports performance, plus early brain evidence on how the method might work.

Training under flicker seemed to help athletes use relevant visual cues more efficiently. Reported gains covered anticipation, quick decisions, and short-term visual memory, mostly in tasks needing fast reactions and precise judgment. Brain wave studies hinted at changes in visual processing areas, though samples were small and measures indirect. Whether gains carry into real competition or last over time remains unproven. The authors call for dose studies, active control groups, and follow-up testing.
pmc-13638480:
Kunal Malhotra and two colleagues published this 2026 narrative review of mental illness in end-stage kidney disease. Roughly a quarter to a third of dialysis patients show clinically significant depression on structured interview, with anxiety close behind. The causes braid together: uremia, anemia, and inflammation on the biological side; job loss, isolation, and money strain on the social side. Diagnosis is tricky because kidney symptoms mimic psychiatric ones and screening tools lean on self-report.

Trials show talk therapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, eases depression, lifts quality of life, and improves treatment adherence in this population. The review also covers drug treatment adjusted for failing kidneys and borrows collaborative care lessons from oncology and primary care. Dialysis centers, however, often lack staff and reimbursement pathways. The authors propose a roadmap for weaving mental health care into dialysis units, carefully separating evidence-based steps from expert opinion.
pmc-13646880:
Danielle Fehr and fourteen colleagues compare gut microbes in adults with atopic dermatitis, the itchy inflammatory skin disease also called eczema, against healthy adults in Tanzania and Switzerland, in a 2026 study. Gut imbalance has been tied to this disease in children, while adult data stayed scarce. Stool from 140 people was read by shotgun gene sequencing. Diet and location were tracked alongside disease status.

Having the disease measurably shifted the gut community, with one species more common in patients and others marking healthy controls. Overall diversity, though, did not differ between groups. Geography left a strong fingerprint too, matching distinct eating habits: one bacterial group thrived in Tanzanian samples, while two others marked Swiss ones. The authors read the results as support for a gut-skin axis and for diet-aware attempts to treat skin disease through the microbiome.
pmc-13647880:
Roi Martin B Pajimna and six colleagues wrap oleuropein, an anti-inflammatory compound from olives, in chitosan-coated fat bubbles to make it survive oral delivery. The compound fights vessel inflammation tied to atherosclerosis, yet it breaks down in water and absorbs poorly. An optimized recipe produced uniform particles with high loading. Cell tests showed the bubbles entered vessel-lining cells readily and left them healthy, and the coating released its cargo slowly in response to acidity.

In mice with triggered vessel inflammation, the coated bubbles lowered two key inflammatory markers in blood more strongly than the free compound or uncoated bubbles at the same dose. Even a tenth of the dose still suppressed the markers substantially, hinting at a dose-sparing effect. Liver and kidney markers stayed normal and organs looked clean. The authors call for direct absorption studies to explain the sparing effect before clinical hopes firm up.
pmc-13647980:
Yu Yu Phua and Bethany Ehlmann build mathematical models for how dark minerals distort Raman laser readings of mixed rocks, a problem for instruments on Earth and Mars alike. Field Raman tools spot a wide patch, so minerals always arrive mixed. When one mineral absorbs strongly, its signal grows nonlinearly and can swamp its neighbors. The team modeled three pairing types, from both-pale to both-dark, then verified the math on lab mixtures of sulfates and clay minerals.

Signal grew in a straight line with abundance only when both minerals were pale. Any dark partner bent the curve. A worked example shows the stakes. A clay's water peak is visible at thirteen percent in a pale host. A dark basalt host needs three times as much clay before the peak registers. The authors offer the models, paired with images or other measurements, to estimate detection limits and abundances.
pmc-13649380:
Alice Gantner and six colleagues probe a hormone sensor called GPER in glioblastoma, the grimmest brain tumour. Men catch it more and die sooner than women, and the gap fades with age, which hints at hormones. The team mined big public cancer data sets, reset to the newest class rules.

High sensor levels meant longer life chiefly in women under 55. Genes that move with the sensor pointed to a slowed cell cycle. In a dish, extra sensor curbed tumour cell growth, which fits the survival link. Three tag sites on the gene, where chemical marks sit, tracked both sensor levels and life span in young women. The team names the sensor a lead for new drugs.
pmc-13650980:
Tracy L Nicholson and one co-author compare drug and zinc resistance in a livestock-associated family of MRSA, the methicillin-resistant staph bacterium, asking whether farm-linked strains seed resistance into human medicine. Their focus is clonal complex 5, comparing human clinical isolates from swine-dense regions, human isolates from people without swine contact, and swine-associated strains.

The zinc resistance gene turned up rarely in all three groups, suggesting that zinc resistance in this bacterium follows lineage more than setting. Swine-associated strains resisted fewer antibiotics than the human groups. The genetic toolkits also differed, including plasmid-carried resistance elements, marking the human and swine families as distinct reservoirs rather than one flowing into the other. The authors conclude that, within this complex, the swine reservoir looks like a minor source of resistance spreading beyond agriculture, while noting the finding covers the isolates examined.
pmc-13651480:
Huan Zhang and six colleagues use Swedish national registers to ask whether a mother's autoimmune disease during pregnancy shadows her child's survival into young adulthood. Earlier work tied such diseases to pregnancy complications, but what happens after infancy was largely uncharted.

Every live birth in Sweden from 2001 to 2014 entered the study, close to one and a half million children followed for a median of just over fifteen years. Children of mothers with autoimmune disease faced a modestly higher risk of death overall, concentrated in infancy and fading with age. Fathers' autoimmune disease showed no clear link, and cousin comparisons weakened the association without reversing it, hinting that shared family factors explain part of the picture. Early birth and small size for gestational age carried a share of the excess. Deaths clustered around perinatal conditions and congenital malformations, consistent with effects beginning before birth.
pmc-13651880:
Jaume Cunill-Subiranas and five colleagues introduce a general method for reshaping magnetic fields without changing the source that produces them. Their framework, called magnetic omniconversion, uses shaped pieces of linear magnetic material placed around a source. The goal is to turn whatever field a magnet or coil happens to make into a precisely chosen field inside a nearby empty region.

Alongside the general recipe, the team gives worked analytical and numerical examples and a proof-of-concept experiment that confirms the idea in practice. Because the conversion does not depend on the source, one setup could serve many different magnets. Possible uses range from magnetic shielding and targeted field delivery to better imaging tools, anywhere a field must match an exact shape rather than an approximation.
pmc-13652080:
Na You and nine colleagues test whether a gene called ARHGAP40 can slow clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common form of kidney cancer. Drawing on large cancer datasets, the team found the gene switched down in tumors, partly through added methylation on its promoter. Laboratory experiments then raised or lowered its activity in cancer cells, and a mouse model checked the effect on tumor growth.

Restoring ARHGAP40 curbed malignant behavior, and the gene physically interacted with RhoA, a known driver of cell movement. Its presence also shifted signals through the PI3K and AKT pathway and changed how cells handled glutamine and oxidative stress, measured through glutathione and reactive oxygen levels. Rescue experiments confirmed the chain of effects, marking ARHGAP40 as a candidate brake on this cancer and a possible guide for new treatment ideas.
pmc-3428680:
Deng, Jiang, Yang, and co-authors present network methods for studying microbial communities. Learning how species in a community interact, and how they respond to change in nature, is a central goal in ecology. Defining network structure in a microbe community is very hard, though.

Microbial diversity is extremely high, and most interactions cannot be observed directly. Their analysis builds networks from survey data, linking species that rise and fall together. Such maps help predict how groups react to pollution, warming, or drugs, and which members hold a community together.
pmc-5076380:
Eldridge, Chan, Campbell, and their co-authors extended the CONSORT statement in 2016 to pilot and feasibility trials. CONSORT is a guideline that improves the transparency and quality of reporting for randomized controlled trials. Pilot and feasibility trials, which test whether a full trial can be run, were often reported poorly.

The extension adapts CONSORT items to these smaller, preparatory studies. It stresses aims such as testing recruitment and procedures, rather than judging treatment effects early. Clear reporting helps funders decide whether a full trial is worth its cost. It also stops weak pilot results from being oversold as evidence of benefit.
pmc-5708080:
Curtis Rueden, Johannes Schindelin, Mark Hiner, and many others described ImageJ2 in 2017. ImageJ is a long-running image analysis program used across biology and beyond. It is loved for its simple macros and the many plug-ins users share.

ImageJ2 rebuilds that base to handle modern image data, which can be huge and have many dimensions. It keeps the old interface and plug-ins working while adding a cleaner core for developers. Labs can keep trusted workflows and still handle new kinds of images. The paper explains the design choices that let old and new parts work together.
pmc-6941980:
Inmaculada Martínez-Reyes and Navdeep Chandel reviewed mitochondrial metabolites in health and disease in 2020. Mitochondria are signaling hubs that help set cell fate, not mere power plants. Their inner cycle, the TCA cycle, sits at the center of that signaling.

Metabolites from the cycle leak signals that steer gene activity, immune behavior, and growth. Broken cycle enzymes cause cancers and metabolic disease through those signals. The review connects classic biochemistry to new findings on cell communication. It reframes a textbook pathway as a control board for physiology. Worked disease examples include cancer, diabetes, and immune disorders driven by faulty cycle signals.
pmc-7299280:
Thomas Rogers and colleagues reported in 2020 that they had isolated powerful antibodies able to block SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. They reasoned that people who had recovered from the infection would carry antibodies shaped by real encounters with the virus. Finding the strongest of those antibodies was the first step toward turning them into a treatment.

The team screened blood from survivors, picked out the antibodies that stopped the virus most completely, and tested the best candidates in a small animal model. The leading antibodies protected the animals from disease. Published during the first year of the pandemic, the study showed that a survivor's own defenses could be copied into a drug, a path several treatments later followed.
pmc-8352980:
Sandra Lopez-Leon and colleagues pooled the evidence in 2021 on the lasting effects of COVID-19, counting more than fifty of them. Their systematic review and meta-analysis gathered studies that followed patients for weeks to months after they had supposedly recovered. They searched major medical literature collections to find every relevant follow up study available at the time.

Combining the results, the authors estimate how common each lingering problem was, from fatigue and breathlessness to hair loss and trouble concentrating. The sheer range of affected organs surprised many readers. The review gave clinicians and health systems an early map of the long tail of the disease, and it underlined the need for dedicated follow up care.
podcast-dannyjones-AziCjLnp780:
Dennis McKenna is a pharmacologist who has studied psychedelic plants for half a century, and the brother of the famed psychonaut Terence McKenna. With Danny Jones, he discusses the beings users of DMT report meeting in that drug's brief, intense state, and the ancient roots he traces for such encounters.

McKenna approaches the entities question as a scientist who has also had the experiences, which makes him an unusual witness. He separates what the chemistry does from what the visions mean, and refuses easy answers in both directions. Jones presses him on whether the beings are real. The episode preserves a serious researcher's fullest public thinking on a subject science mostly avoids, delivered with more honesty about uncertainty than either believers or skeptics usually allow.
podcast-dannyjones-EpW2lFqxx80:
Robert Salas was an Air Force officer stationed at a nuclear missile base in 1967 when, by his account, a glowing object hovered over the gate and his missiles went offline. On Danny Jones's podcast, the former nuclear warfare officer argues that something disturbing is still interfering with America's nuclear arsenal.

Salas has told his story to Congress and journalists for decades, and other veterans have reported similar shutdowns. The military's explanations differ, and no physical proof has settled the matter. What the episode offers is a trained officer's testimony, consistent over a lifetime, about the most sensitive weapons on earth. Jones questions him closely. Listeners must decide what such testimony is worth, which is exactly the problem the disclosure debate keeps circling.
podcast-dannyjones-LQZtTgA1N80:
Physicist Matthew Szydagis works on dark matter detection deep underground. He joins Danny Jones to discuss a startling extension of his field. It is evidence, as he presents it, that UFOs have been present on earth for a million years. His path runs from particle physics to the fossil and historical record of strange objects.

Szydagis applies a detector scientist's habits to fringe material, asking what would count as data and what is only story. Jones follows him from laboratory practice to ancient reports. The million-year claim is Szydagis's own reading, not his field's consensus, and the episode labels it by its framing. Listeners get something rare in this series: a working experimentalist explaining, carefully and on the record, why he thinks the UFO evidence deserves laboratory-grade attention.
podcast-joerogan-LeCpHugyI80:
Biogerontologist Aubrey de Grey joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 638, an early entry in the show's science run. De Grey argues that aging is a kind of damage the body can, in time, be repaired against. When this aired, the idea still sounded like science fiction to most ears.

He lays out the seven kinds of damage he wants medicine to fix, and his guess at the timeline. Rogan asks what a world without aging would do to work, family, and meaning. The episode preserves a bold claim at an early stage, from the man who made ending aging a public cause.
podcast-joerogan-RD-9Ghvt480:
Duncan Trussell's episode 1313 of the Joe Rogan Experience is another entry in the show's longest friendship. Trussell, comedian and host of a family-hour podcast of his own, treats Rogan's studio like a second home. Their talks need no news hook to get going.

The conversation drifts across psychedelic tales, the puzzle of the self, and the jokes Trussell builds from both. Rogan keeps one foot on the ground, telling his own stories between the flights. The episode is a pure example of the pair's chemistry, the blend of stand-up and soul talk that made Trussell a signature guest.
rochester-poems-1680:
The Works of the Right Honourable John, Earl of Rochester, are printed here for the booksellers of London and Westminster, in an edition dated 1718 and priced at one shilling. Its title page promises satires, songs, translations, and other occasional poems. A Satire against Mankind leads the contents, at page three.

Tunbridge-Wells, a satire, follows, with an imitation of Horace and A Satire against Marriage. A Letter from Artemisa in the Town to Cloe in the Country and The Maim'd Debauchee stand in the list. Upon Nothing, The Advice, The Discovery, and an elegy from Ovid's Amours show the range of Rochester's wit, grave and wild by turns.
scheele-air-and-fire-1780:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele was a Swedish apothecary who built a great lab life on a small wage. His work on air and fire came out in German in 1777, then in English in 1780. He did his best work in small towns, far from the great schools.

Scheele found the gas we now call oxygen on his own, and named it fire air. He printed his claim late, so the fame went to men who spoke first in public. The book is his own record, and it shows a fine hand at trials.
shabistari-gulshan-i-raz-whinfield-1880:
Mahmud Shabistari was a Persian poet of Tabriz. In 1317 he answered seventeen questions on Sufi doctrine in verse, and he called the poem Gulshan-i Raz, the Rose Garden of Mystery. E. H. Whinfield published his English version in 1880, with an introduction and notes drawn from the great commentary of Lahiji. The Persian text pages are left out of this copy; the English matter is complete.

Question by question, Shabistari treats the self, the heart, the beloved, wine, and the tavern of ruin as signs of the soul's road to God. His answers became the pocket summa of Persian Sufism. Students memorized the couplets for six centuries. Whinfield's version was the first door into the garden for English readers.
sixth-and-seventh-books-of-moses-1880:
The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses, in this 1880 English edition prepared under Johann Scheibel's name, is a German folk grimoire ascribed to Moses. A grimoire is a handbook of spells, seals, and conjurations for practical use. No book of spells traveled further in American folk practice.

Its pages give seals, psalms, and formulas for healing, finding treasure, binding enemies, and turning luck. German settlers carried it into Pennsylvania Dutch country, and from there it passed into African-American hoodoo practice. Conjure workers treated the book itself as a power object, kept wrapped and hidden like a weapon.
sixth-seventh-books-moses-1880:
The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses claim to print the lost magic books of Moses himself. This English edition of 1880 carried the German folk text to American readers. Packed with Solomonic seals, psalm charms, and conjurations, it became the most famous American grimoire of its kind.

In Pennsylvania Dutch country, the book became the backbone of pow-wow magic. Healers used its seals and words for cures, protection, and treasure. Copies passed through farm families as working tools, sometimes feared as much as valued. The 1880 printing fixed the text that spread through German America. Charms and cures from that world are still whispered where the book is kept.
the-afghan-wars-1839-42-and-1878-80: Archibald Forbes wrote The Afghan Wars 1839-42 and 1878-80. Portraits and plans support the text. A front plate shows Sir Frederick Roberts. Part one lists the first war's chapters. The March to Cabul comes first. Two years of occupation follow. The Road to Ruin and The Catastrophe come next. The siege and defence of Jellalabad follows. Retribution and Rescue closes that part. Part two opens the second war. Two campaigns and a lull before the storm start it.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Old Age and Death, the closing part of Spanish Passions in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, is not Casanova's own narrative but an editorial appendix and supplement. It follows the 1894 London edition in Arthur Machen's translation, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. The editors admit uncertainty: the author may have died before finishing, or the concluding volumes were destroyed, or the manuscript fell into bad hands. Materials for continuing the story are extremely fragmentary.

What can be told comes largely from the Prince de Ligne's memoirs. Pardoned at last, Casanova returned to Venice as a secret agent of the State Inquisitors, in plain language a spy, and made an indifferent one. Later he became librarian to Count Waldstein at the Castle of Dux, near Teplitz. There he spent fourteen years, resenting bad coffee, ill-cooked macaroni, barking dogs, and small tables.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-30:
Headed volume thirty-two in its own pages, though the record calls it volume thirty, this portion covers 1579 and 1580 in chapter two. Parma feints at Antwerp, invests Maastricht, and negotiates with Walloon envoys in his camp amid festivities that produce a treaty of reconciliation.

Religious tumults shake Antwerp and Utrecht while Orange enforces religious peace. At Maastricht mining and countermining, attacks on two gates, and gradual encroachment end with the town taken and a horrible massacre, followed by solemn thanksgiving. Negotiation and patient siege-craft advance together steadily under Parma's guiding hand.
tob-0144-56880:
After the sweeping systems of the first two volumes, volume three of The Secret Doctrine gathers looser material. Blavatsky left essays, fragments, and notes on occult history and symbolism, much of it unfinished at her death in 1891. Editors shaped the mass into a third volume.

Readers find teachings on hidden adepts, the inner meaning of symbols, and the secret history of religions. The tone shifts from chapter to chapter, since the pieces were written for different purposes. Fans prize the volume for hints dropped nowhere else. Newcomers fare better starting with volume one, then returning here.
tob-0180:
Cairo, 1904: Crowley said a voice named Aiwass dictated the Book of the Law to him over three days. The short, fierce text became the central scripture of Thelema, his new religion. Its best-known line lays down the law of the new age: do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law.

Three chapters speak in the voices of Egyptian gods, mixing command, prophecy, and riddling verse. Followers treat each line as charged with meaning; critics see a curiosity of occult history. Either way, few short texts have founded so much. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-9480:
Pindar, the leading lyric poet of ancient Greece, wrote odes to honor men who won at the Olympic Games. The Olympian Odes praise victors in running, wrestling, boxing, and chariot racing. Morice's English translation is the version named for this entry.

Each ode mixes praise of the winner with myths of gods and heroes linked to his city or family. Pindar warns winners to stay humble, since gods give success and can take it away. His grand, dense verse set the pattern for praise poetry in the West, and later poets from Horace onward studied him closely.
un-ga-res-a-69-80:
Peace around the Mediterranean Sea is the broad theme of Resolution A/69/80, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The lands that ring the sea, the text holds, bear the chief duty for its peace, safety, and joint work. It welcomes the steps of Euro-Mediterranean states to deepen their ties, above all in the fight against terror, through the joint code agreed at Barcelona in 2005.

Past pledges and meetings of the shore states are recalled in force. A fresh push came in 2008, when the Paris summit launched a stronger pact, the Union for the Mediterranean. The vote keeps the sea's peace framed as a shared task, from Gibraltar to the Levant.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Hosted under the Resolution 180 label, the text here is the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. The General Assembly adopted the treaty on 18 December 1979, through resolution 34/180. An opening note explains the convention's background. It turns the earlier declaration against discrimination against women into a binding treaty. An expert committee watches over it.

The articles define discrimination against women. They then require states to ban it in law and in daily life. They cover voting and public office, nationality, and schooling. They also cover jobs and equal pay, and health care. They cover equality in marriage and family life. They call for an end to traffic in women.

Resolution 69/80 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns security and cooperation in the Mediterranean region. It treats Mediterranean security as closely tied to European and international security. It calls on states of the region to join disarmament and non-proliferation instruments. It calls on them to report military spending openly. It encourages joint action against terrorism, organized crime and drug trafficking. A further report is requested from the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1380:
Western Sahara's referendum mission received a three-month renewal in late 2001. On 27 November 2001 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 28 February 2002. The Secretary-General had written to the Council that month. The Council recalled its backing of his envoy's search for a settlement. The dispute between Morocco and the Polisario Front remained unresolved.

The Secretary-General owed an interim report by 15 January 2002. A fuller assessment had to arrive by 18 February. The Council stayed seized of the matter. Short renewals like this one kept the ceasefire under watch. They also reflected how far the parties were from agreeing on a vote.
un-sc-res-1480:
Timor-Leste's support mission gained a final full year in May 2003. On 19 May 2003 the Security Council extended UNMISET until 20 May 2004. The Council praised the Timorese people and government. Their young state was building its institutions on democratic values. It also praised the mission's work under the Secretary-General's special representative. UNMISET was helping to train the national administration and police.

The extension kept United Nations backing in place for a second year of independence. The mission's name recalled its task, support for East Timor. Its staff worked beside Timorese officials rather than ruling directly. That marked a change from the earlier transitional administration. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter.
un-sc-res-1580: From 2004 comes Resolution 1580, a Security Council act preserved through an English Wikisource transcription of the official record. The document's authority rests on its form as much as its content: a single agreed text, voted once, binding in effect. The entry keeps that text complete, including the closing calls for follow-up reports.
un-sc-res-1680:
Lebanon's sovereignty resolution gained a progress check on 17 May 2006. The Secretary-General's third report on resolution 1559 (2004), dated 18 April 2006, noted real gains through the Lebanese national dialogue. Other parts lagged. Militias were not broken up or disarmed. State control did not run over all territory, and arms had moved into Lebanon for militias in the past six months. Beirut's prime minister had addressed the Council in April.

The Council repeated its call to apply resolution 1559 in full. All states and parties named in the report were told to cooperate at once. Syria was strongly encouraged to answer Lebanon's request for border talks and diplomatic ties. The Council praised Lebanon's steps against arms smuggling and welcomed the national dialogue's decision to disarm Palestinian militias outside the camps. It backed the Secretary-General and his envoy in their work.
un-sc-res-1780: In 2007 the Council voted Resolution 1780 into the record, and the text is preserved here via English Wikisource. The fifteen members' product is a single document with two voices: the preamble's measured assessment and the operative part's direct instructions. Readers who need to know what the Council required can go straight to those numbered lines.
un-sc-res-180:
African states brought a complaint to the Council. Thirty-two of them raised the case of lands under Portuguese rule. Resolution 180 was adopted on 31 July 1963. It recalls Assembly texts on those lands. The Assembly had called them Non-Self-Governing Territories. That status comes from the UN Charter. It points toward full freedom in time.

The Council confirms Assembly Resolution 1514. That text dates from 1960. It called for quick steps to hand power to local peoples. Their freely stated wishes were to guide the change. Race, creed, and colour were not to bar anyone. The Council also rejects Portugal's stance. Portugal called its colonies overseas parts of itself. The Council says that stance clashes with these principles.
un-sc-res-1880:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1880, adopted on 30 July 2009. A presidential election was set for 29 November 2009 under the Ouagadougou peace deal. Key reunification steps had to finish by September, two months before the vote. The peacekeeping mission and the French force backing it were near the end of their terms.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends both mandates until 31 January 2010. The mission must help the parties finish the remaining peace tasks. Disarmament of militias and former fighters continues. The electoral commission gets technical and logistical support for a safe vote. The mission also guards human rights work and helps restore police and courts across the country.
un-sc-res-280:
Lebanon brought the Council to Resolution 280, adopted on 19 May 1970 by eleven votes to none, with four abstentions. Israeli forces had struck deep into Lebanon on 12 May. The Council had already demanded a full pullout that same day. Earlier warnings after past raids had gone unheeded.

The Council calls the attack planned ahead and large in scale. It condemns Israel for breaking its duties under the Charter. It deplores Israel's failure to obey the earlier texts on Lebanon. Such armed attacks, the Council declares, can no longer be stood for. If they recur, the Council warns, it will weigh firm steps under the Charter to enforce its word.
un-sc-res-380:
Morocco's Green March entered Western Sahara in November 1975. Hundreds of thousands of civilians walked into the territory. The Council had twice told Morocco to call the march off. Its president had appealed directly to the king. The march went ahead anyway. On 6 November 1975 the Council deplored that it had taken place. The situation, it said, had seriously deteriorated.

Morocco had to withdraw all the marchers from the territory at once. All parties had to avoid acts that could raise tension further. They also had to cooperate with the Secretary-General. The Assembly's own review of the territory's status ran in parallel. Spain left within months, and Morocco took control of most of the territory.
un-sc-res-580:
South Africa's deadly raid into Lesotho was condemned on 30 December 1985. Lesotho's letter of 23 December told of unprovoked and premeditated killings. Six South African refugees and three Lesotho nationals lay dead in Maseru. The Council recalled resolution 527 (1982), passed after an earlier South African raid on the same city.

The Council strongly condemned the killings and the violence done against Lesotho, in flagrant breach of its sovereignty. South Africa had to pay full and adequate compensation for the loss of life and damage. Lesotho's right to give sanctuary to the victims of apartheid was reaffirmed. Member states were asked to give Lesotho urgent economic help to strengthen its power to receive and keep refugees. South Africa was called to settle its disputes by peaceful means. It also had to honor its pledge not to destabilize its neighbors or let its soil serve attacks on them.
un-sc-res-80:
Kashmir's demilitarization was pressed by the Security Council on 14 March 1950. The United Nations Commission for India and Pakistan had won agreement on a cease-fire, a cease-fire line from July 1949, and a plebiscite plan for the state's future. A Canadian general's talks on troop withdrawals had been reported to the Council. Both governments won praise for their statesmanlike steps so far.

The Council called on India and Pakistan to prepare and carry out a demilitarization programme within five months. It decided to appoint a United Nations Representative to push the process and help settle remaining disputes. The two governments were told to keep the cease-fire faithfully and guard law and order. The Council thanked the commission and the general for their work. It agreed the commission would be wound up one month after both sides reported the representative's appointment accepted.
un-sc-res-980: Judge Sir Robert Yewdall Jennings resigned from the International Court of Justice in 1995. His departure took effect on 10 July that year. On 22 March 1995 the Security Council set the date to fill the vacancy. The election would be held on 12 July 1995. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was in its forty-ninth session. The short text performs only that scheduling task.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Sahara envoy's compromise talks frame this extension of 2001. On 27 November, the Council adopted Resolution 1380 without dissent. It took note of the Secretary-General's letter of 12 November. The vote mission, MINURSO, was marking time that year. The envoy was testing if Morocco and the Polisario Front could take a deal instead of the stalled vote.

The text extends MINURSO's mandate to 28 February 2002. An interim report is due by 15 January. A full assessment must follow by 18 February. The Council stays seized of the matter in the meantime. Those February reports listed four paths for the territory. They set the agenda for debate through 2002 and 2003.

One year after Timor-Leste's independence, the Council kept its support mission there running. Resolution 1480 passed unanimously on 19 May 2003. The mission was called UNMISET. It was helping the young state build courts and police. It also supported administration and defense forces. Slowly, it was handing power to local officials.

The mandate now ran to 20 May 2004, the planned finish date. The text underlines police training as a top priority. It welcomes better ties between Timor-Leste and Indonesia. It also presses for border agreements. And it demands justice for serious crimes committed during the violence of 1999.

A military mutiny on 6 October 2004, in which senior officers were assassinated, shook Guinea-Bissau's fragile transition, and on 22 December 2004 its United Nations office is extended and reshaped. UNOGBIS, the Peace-Building Support Office, had watched over the transition. Legislative elections had been held that March, but the new institutions remained weak.

UNOGBIS is renewed as a special political mission with a revised mandate. The office is to help strengthen state institutions, support the rule of law and the fight against impunity, and assist the transition toward planned presidential elections. The Secretary-General is asked to review the office's work, and the National Assembly is urged to act on reforms, including in the security sector.

Resolution 1680, passed on 17 May 2006, pushes Lebanon and Syria on the loose ends of a 2004 text. That text, 1559, had told all armed groups in Lebanon to lay down their arms. It had told all foreign troops to leave. Talks among Lebanon's own leaders had moved some points on. But armed groups still held their guns. Fresh arms had crossed into Lebanon in the past six months.

The Council urged Syria to say yes to Lebanon's wish for two things. One was a clear line for their shared border. The other was full, normal ties, with envoys in each other's capitals. It also told all sides to carry out 1559 in full, and asked for fresh news on progress.

Haiti's stabilization mission, MINUSTAH, is extended until 15 October 2008 on 15 October 2007. Haiti had completed its local and municipal elections in April 2007, the final round of a long electoral cycle. Progress on security, the rule of law, and development are linked as gains that reinforce each other.

The Secretary-General's plan to reconfigure the mission, trimming its military side and strengthening its police, is endorsed. MINUSTAH is to keep backing the Haitian National Police, help reform the justice and prison systems, and support border management. It is also asked to give technical expertise to the government and to work with the United Nations country team on aid and recovery across the country.

Portugal's African territories are taken up on 31 July 1963, in a case brought by thirty-two African member states. The General Assembly had declared the territories Non-Self-Governing and had called for power to pass to their peoples at once. The Council's own Angola resolution of 1961 had gone unheeded by Lisbon.

The Assembly's declaration on ending colonial rule is confirmed, and Portugal's policies are affirmed to run against the Charter. Lisbon is called on to grant the territories' peoples their rights, including self-determination leading to independence. All states are asked to stop giving Portugal any help that lets it continue repression, and to block arms sales for that purpose. The Secretary-General is to report by 31 October 1963.

Côte d'Ivoire's election date is locked in as UNOCI is renewed in Resolution 1880, adopted on 30 July 2009. Under the Ouagadougou Political Agreement the first round of the presidential election was set for 29 November 2009. Voter registration was complete. But the provisional voters list was still unpublished. Human rights violations, including sexual violence, persisted.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews UNOCI's mandate until 31 January 2010, centred on supporting free, open, fair, and transparent elections. It insists the Ivorian actors respect the 29 November date. It says any postponement would break faith with the Ouagadougou Agreement. It demands the provisional voters list be published before the end of August 2009. The Secretary-General's Special Representative must certify the voters list and every electoral stage under the five-criteria framework. The Council warns it is ready to impose targeted sanctions on anyone threatening the electoral process.

Resolution 2580, adopted on 8 June 2021, is a single operative sentence from the Security Council. It decides who should lead the United Nations next. Having considered the question, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that António Guterres be appointed Secretary-General of the United Nations for a second term. The term runs from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2026. Under the UN Charter, the General Assembly makes the appointment on the Council's recommendation, so this brief text carries the full weight of the choice.

Israeli forces had struck deep into Lebanon in May 1970. Resolution 280, adopted on 19 May 1970, was the Council's angry response. Eleven members backed it. Colombia, Nicaragua, Sierra Leone, and the United States abstained. Both Lebanon and Israel had presented their cases.

The Council judged the attack planned and large in scale. It condemned Israel for striking in breach of the Charter. It repeated a solemn warning: further attacks would not be tolerated. If they came, members would consider firm steps to enforce their decisions. The text also mourns the deaths and damage caused by the fighting.

A vast march of Moroccan crowds crossed into Western Sahara in November 1975. King Hassan II had called the Green March to claim the land. Spain was set to quit the colony. The Council had begged the king to call the march off. He did not. Resolution 380 passed by common consent on 6 November 1975, the day the march crossed the line.

The Council voiced its grief that the march had gone ahead. Morocco had to pull all marchers out of the land at once. All sides had to work with the UN chief. His task came from two texts passed that fall. The vote did no good in the short run. Morocco held the land. A war with the Polisario Front ran for years. The file marks the start of a long, stuck fight.

Resolution 580, adopted on 30 December 1985, condemns a South African raid into Lesotho. The Council heard Lesotho's foreign minister describe unplanned, deliberate killings blamed on South Africa. Six South African refugees and three Lesotho nationals had been killed. Members said the attack broke Lesotho's sovereignty and was meant to punish the small kingdom for sheltering people fleeing apartheid.

The Council strongly condemns the killings and demands that South Africa pay full compensation for the lives lost and the damage done. It backs Lesotho's right to give shelter to victims of apartheid and asks member states to send urgent economic help so Lesotho can care for refugees. It demands steps to tear down apartheid and asks for a small UN presence in Maseru to watch the situation.

Resolution 80, adopted on 14 March 1950 by eight votes to none with two abstentions, restarts the UN effort on Kashmir. A UN commission for India and Pakistan had produced ceasefire and plebiscite agreements, and a Canadian general, A. G. L. McNaughton, had explored the remaining gaps in talks with both governments. Hostilities had stopped in January 1949 and a ceasefire line was drawn that July.

The Council praised both governments for the steps already taken, including agreeing that Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz would serve as plebiscite administrator. It then moved to replace the commission with a single United Nations representative, who would press ahead with demilitarizing the state so the promised vote on Kashmir's future could be held.

Judge Sir Robert Yewdall Jennings, a British jurist on the International Court of Justice, resigned his seat effective 10 July 1995. Resolution 980, adopted on 22 March 1995, exists for one narrow reason: fixing the date on which his replacement on the world court would be elected.

The members chose 12 July 1995, two days after the resignation took hold. Voting would take place in parallel, at a Security Council meeting and during the General Assembly's forty-ninth session, because judges of the Court must be elected by both bodies. The text also records, in formal language, that Jennings's departure left a gap covering only the remainder of his original term.
wallace-island-life-1880:
In Island Life, published in 1880, Wallace asks why islands hold such strange mixes of plants and animals. He draws on his years in Malaysia and on reports from sailors and collectors worldwide. Islands, he argues, are natural test cases for how life spreads and changes. The book grew from the same travels as his Malay Archipelago.

Wallace weighs two answers: creatures rafted or flew across seas, or old land bridges once joined now-split lands. He uses ice ages, sea depth, and fossils to test each island case by case. His work founded island biogeography and still guides the study of island species.
willis-improved-chart-for-recording-a-de: The scan pages here show the title pages, partly garbled, of a character chart by Professor A. B. Willis, and nothing else is present. The chart was made to record a reading of character by phrenology, physiognomy, and physiology. Those three arts judged a person by head shape, face, and body. Cameron, Amberg and Company printed it in Chicago in 1880. A Library of Congress stamp marks the copy. The full title repeats on a second page, calling the chart improved. No filled-in reading appears in these pages.
wood-order-zeuglodontia-nature-1880:
Searles Wood makes a bold claim for the sea serpent in his Nature note of 1880. Wood was a sage of old life forms. Ships oft told of a great long necked beast in far seas. He holds the beast could be a zeuglodon. Such whales of old ages had snake like frames. Thought long dead, one may yet live in deep seas men can't sweep.

His note is brief, grave, and writ for sages, not crowds. It gave the serpent a place in the tree of life. The row it sparked ran for years. It is a key text of that row.
yeates-affidavit-nsa-1980:
The National Security Agency fought in court to keep 156 UFO reports sealed, and its sworn word is this file. The in camera affidavit of Eugene Yeates, dated October 9, 1980, was sworn in the case of CAUS against the NSA. Yeates was chief of the agency's Office of Policy.

He tells the judge, in a closed filing, why each of the reports must stay dark. The papers were communications intelligence tied to foreign air and spy craft. Freed at last in 2009, with black bars still in place, the affidavit is the core file of NSA UFO secrecy. It shows the agency guarding its silence by law.
zola-attack-on-mill-1880:
Edmund Gosse translated The Attack on the Mill and its companion war sketches. Zola wrote the title tale in 1880, a decade after the Franco-Prussian War. The setting is a village mill on the day of a wedding feast.

Soldiers seize the mill in the midst of the joy, and the feast turns to slaughter. Few war stories in any language match its force and pity. The sketches around it extend the same bleak view of war's waste. Anger burns through every page at lives thrown away for pride and flags. Readers who know Zola only from the long novels will find his power in brief form here.
zollner-transcendental-physics-1880:
Johann Zollner claimed a fourth span of space in Transcendental Physics, his book in English from 1880. Zollner was a chief of star lore at Leipzig. He sat with Slade, a famed seer, and saw knots tied in sealed cords, rings passed through wood, and goods moved in ways no hand in our space could work, he swore.

A fourth span, with souls in it, is his bold key. Peers cried fraud and shame. Fans hailed a new age of science. The book is the row's most famed flash point. Its claims still spark heat.
